speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to the provisions of Standing Order 43, I request the unanimous consent of the House to present a motion dealing with an important matter of national urgency.
Given the fact that under the new dairy policy Quebec industrial milk producers stand to lose over $100 million in income; that, by the Minister of Agriculture's own admission, producers have generally respected their quotas and are in no way responsible for the present surpluses, and that, consequently, those producers should not be penalized for an over-production to which they did not contribute, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Joliette (Mr. La Salle):
That the government accept the principle of a compensatory subsidy to those Quebec milk producers who, in the last dairy year, have respected their quotas, or that it exempt them from the pertinent provisions of its dairy policy; that, in addition, the government defer application of its new policy on the feed grains transport subsidy until such time as the producers concerned have been consulted and the new substitute programs promised by the government have been announced.

We are also trying to envision how it can be integrated into the present system, and most of all, how it can be used to generate more revenues in the broadcasting industry, thus enhancing our position in producing better quality Canadian programs.

speechtext: for leave to introduce Bill C-440, respecting the domestic and industrial use of solar energy.

speechtext: Explain.

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING DOMESTIC AND INDUSTRIAL USE OF SOLAR ENERGY
speechtext:
Briefly, Mr. Speaker, the reasons for introducing this bill are the following. Time is running out before non-renewable resources will have been depleted. Future generations of Canadians, and their energy requirements, depend upon decisions made in this decade. The potential offered by renewable resources, such as the sun, needs to be pursued vigorously now. Solar power heating offers an opportunity for the development of a new Canadian industry. Considerable strides are being made in other industrial nations, particularly the United States. We must develop the solar heating technology suited to the Canadian climate.
The purpose of the bill is to establish an institute of solar energy applications. The institute would undertake intensive research leading to the development of a technology that will permit the use of solar energy.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my feeling indeed is that the best speech in this debate is now being made outside this House, a few steps from here on Parliament Hill, because some 10,000 farmers are now expressing to the government their dissatisfaction and anger with the inequities now being caused against the farming industry in Quebec, Ontario and elsewhere.
I hope their vibrant speech will be heard by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald), the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) and the government as a whole.
Before starting these comments, I had an opportunity to state, in a motion under Standing Order 43, that Quebec's industrial milk producers will face a loss of revenue totalling more than $100 million. I also indicated that by the Minister of Agriculture's (Mr. Whelan) own admission, those producers respected their quotas and are in no way responsible for the current overproduction. Therefore, they should not be penalized for something they did not contribute to. Mr. Speaker, I would extend to the Minister of Finance the usual congratulations for his tour de force in presenting us with a non-budget, for the know-how with which attempted to have us accept his wait and see approach as an action-oriented approach. Of course I share the views of the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens). I was pleased to second the non-confidence motion that he put forward as regards a budget speech of which he underlined the mistakes and deficiencies.
* (1510)
Even though our party has no majority in the House, it is obvious from what we hear from every region of this country that it reflects the view of the majority of Canadian taxpayers in this debate. The very fact that Liberal members have publicly indicated their reservations about the government policy is a very strong indication that it does not have the support of the public at large.
How times have changed, Mr. Speaker! Two years ago, we were in the midst of an electoral campaign and the Prime Minister was still refusing to recognize the impending danger of inflation. He was openly laughing at the program that the Progressive Conservative Party was suggesting. Fifteen months later, on October 13, 1975, the government leader appeared on the national radio and television network to recognize publicly that one year earlier he had cheated the people. He was introducing it as his party's initiative, but scamping it in such a way and with such clumsiness that today, everybody has to admit that his administration is a complete failure.
In his non-confidence motion, our party is asking most hon. members to support it because nothing justifies us to
June 3, 1976

believe that the incapacity the government has shown since 1968, and which is aggravating every week, has suddenly turned into expertise. Nothing allows us to think that the congenital weakness of cabinet members has suddenly turned into energy. We are always faced with the same inert and inefficient cabinet and getting rid of them as soon as possible would do this country great service.
The mockery of a budget which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) introduced on May 25 is a further indication of this inefficiency. In this regard, some people have mentioned a status quo. Reality is even worse: We have here a policy of ultra-conservatism. The Minister of Finance was satisfied with making minor adjustments in the hope that others, the United States in particular, will come to his rescue. Being unable to conceive dynamic initiatives that would meet our actual requirements, the minister is merely following the lead of foreign economies.
When tax incentives were needed to stimulate the shaky recovery that was emerging, the minister only granted very small benefits to small businesses, but he further whittled down corporate profits. He has increased a little bit the deductions for child care and retirement savings plans, but, as a whole, he has not submitted to us any program that would really contribute to improve the difficult economic conditions this country is facing.

I deeply regret that the government did not see its way clear to provide this country with a limited quantity of something which is all too rare these days-a little bit of hope. No one wanted extravagant promises. Our leader and our party have pushed for realistic spending and for realistic spending restraint on the part of the federal government. But this does not mean the exclusion of hope-hope for the working people who wonder when controls will begin to operate in favour of the average man; hope for the small businessmen who wonder when exports and real economic activity will allow for expansion; hope for students who want nothing more greedy or self-centred than a chance to work their way through college or university; hope for the young people in the maritimes, Quebec and elsewhere who would like to find work, purchase a home and build a future.
I share with the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) belief in the need for a responsible and balanced budget. But that does not necessarily mean a budget which is dull and unimaginative. Budgets are more than a prognosis of a government's spending activity; they are more than indicators of what the country can expect in terms of taxes and assistance. They are assessments of economic health and of the capacity of the nation to produce the wealth needed to sustain and improve the quality of life for its citizens. Where are the programs to produce more jobs? Where are the programs to assist the poor, the needy, the disunited?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Read it.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Where is the humanity, where is the compassion? I believe the budget is one drawn up by men who revel in the status quo; indeed, they are prisoners of the status quo. It is a budget devoid of humanity, compassion, hope and optimism. If history is to say anything about the difference between our party and the party opposite on budgetary matters in the year 1976, I hope it might say that
The Budget-Mr. Wagner
we in the Progressive Conservative party believed in the economic capacity of this nation, when the government did not; that we believed in the average man and woman in this country, when the government did not; that we believed in the future of this country, when the government did not.

Mr. Speaker, there is no need to be an expert on economic matters to be concerned about a deficit of the order of $5 billion. Nobody can accept either expenditures which amount to $42 billion. As far as its spending is concerned, the government has not made any worthwhile cutbacks. And what about the adverse trade balance which amount to an astronomical figure.
Everyone is concerned about the government decision to maintain the interest rates at an artificially high level. It is true that after its long-standing slackness, the government simply had to check the growth of the money supply, but this belated policy can only hinder every more a shaky economic recovery. Without tax incentives, without tax cuts, especially for low income groups, this economic recovery will not be enough to absorb a significant number of the 761,000 unemployed registered last month.
This government is resigned to maintaining the unemployment rate to its present level. I say resigned but it is patently obvious that this government depends on unemployment to reduce inflationary pressures. It comes back to the old classical method: create unemployment to fight inflation, let thousands of workers idle so that demand will not be increased, all this in the hope that the inflation rate will get down to 8 per cent this year, a level which is not even reassuring.
So the minister resorts to the unemployment-inflation trade off. What a philosophy! What contempt for distributive justice, what irresponsibility in front of the dangers that all those Canadians maintained in unwarranted poverty represent for social peace. We have a good example this afternoon on Parliament Hill, we can see how angry citizens can get when they are provoqued to such extent by an irresponsible, insensitive, intransigent and unfair government.
If this is the new society promised by the Prime Minister, it deserves to abort like the just society about which, incidentally, we no longer hear anything. In its fight against inflation, this government maintains a false feeling of security in the public. It knows very well, for instance, that the recent and modest dip of the consumer price index will not last very long. The expected increase in oil prices will be felt this fall and next year in a wide range of products and services, particularly in essential sectors like food, housing and transportation.
Furthermore, in his predictions the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) did not take into account a new element which in recent months has influenced the cost of living- the almost general increase in provincial taxes and especially municipal rates. Without adequate revenues, the municipalities will continue to demand more from the homeowner. And how could it be otherwise? In 1975, local governments' revenues went up by only 13.5 per cent while their expenditures increased by 15.8 per cent. The small
95S68-S9'/2

June 3, 1976
The Budget-Mr. Wagner
owner has also become one of the greatest victims of this government's policy.
Mr. Speaker, a moment ago, I spoke of unemployment. The budget offers no hope to the 11,000 textile workers who have been laid off in the last 18 months. I am sorry the minister did not concern himself with the critical crisis the textile industry is now going through, an industry that is very important to the provinces of Ontario and Quebec and, in particular, allow me to point it out, to my riding of Saint-Hyacinthe.
It is urgent that the government should hear at last the cries of alarm Quebec and Ontario authorities have just put out. It is high time it take into consideration the admonitions of the Senate Committee on Banking, Trade and Commerce and that it answer the dramatic appeal of the Congress of Democratic Unions.
Despite some initial success, after the 1970 reform, the textile sector fell back into stagnation. Still, thanks to increased productivity, it proved it could get back on its feet. What it lacks now for a decisive impulse, is very simply a sensible policy on the part of the government. Under the pretext of international commitments and aid to the underdeveloped countries, the government authorizes the import of textile products to a far greater extent than do other countries which have also signed the same agreements.
Studies have shown that the main problem facing our textile industry is not a lack of markets, but massive imports. Imports now account for 54 per cent of our domestic market, compared with 12 per cent for the United States, 10 per cent for Japan and 20 per cent for the European Common Market. It is therefore not surprising under theses circumstances that the textile industry has been constantly on the decrease in Canada. From 1973 to 1974, in a single year, the number of workers went down from 102,000 to 86,000. From 1969 to 1976, 33 plants closed down and 6,000 workers became chronically unemployed.
I know that the government talks about the need to help developing countries. However, at the present time, the textiles which constitute the worst threat for our industries come mostly from highly industrialized countries. I accept the fact that we must help developing countries by accepting their textile products, but instead of opening our boundaries indiscriminately, would it not be more logical to accept foreign textiles in a ratio inversely proportional to the standard of living of the country we want to help? In this way, the most needy would receive our help and we would be protected against competition from the wealthiest countries.
One thing is certain, the present voluntary quota system must be completely reviewed. The government should be more realistic and abandon a policy which is now leading our textile industry to a slow death. The Senate Comittee on Banking, Trade and Commerce and the CSD have shown the way: to sign, like the United States, bilateral agreements concerning the level and nature of textiles that we shall accept; to establish long-term objectives in relation to the potential of the textile industry, both as concerns production and employment. We could thus eliminate the uncertainty which is drying up investments and discouraging the workers. As Mr Yvan Guay wrote in the

newspaper La Presse of May, 19, Canada must finally stop playing boy scout because, and I quote:
For Canada to assume alone the responsibility for a world free-trade policy would be ridiculous and the more so since clothing, like food, is a basic product. No country can ever rely excessively on foreign nations for its food and its clothing ... That is why the textile and clothing industry, like agriculture, must be more or less subsidized if we do not want its workers to become under-proletarians.
And while I am talking about unemployment, Mr. Speaker, there is reason to be concerned about the general economic situation in the metropolitan area of Montreal once the works for the Olympic Games are finished. Economists, business and labour spokesmen have brought to the attention of authorities the need to avoid massive unemployment in the building sector. Layoffs have already begun and more will soon follow.
The situation appears all the more serious because the government of Quebec has just ordered that the work on the subway extension be suspended and the government in Ottawa comes in with postponements on the completion of Place Guy Favreau and the new postal terminal and cuts back on its budget for public or harbour works in the metropolis. It is imperative that federal, provincial and municipal authorities get together on an urgent basis to set up a works program capable of absorbing the greater part of the manpower made available. Construction workers in greater Montreal must be protected from massive unemployment. It would be unfair to let them bear the load of budget restraint. If expenditures must be cut back, let it not be by denying those workers their livelihood.
Just a word about Loto Canada for which the government is asking for $5 million in interim supply. I accept that in principle but on very specific conditions. The government must not permanently interfere with an area that is better left with the provinces and in which they have indeed taken the initiative. We are pleased to see that Loto Canada will contribute to make up the deficit of the Olympic Games in Montreal and will also bring a substantial contribution to those to be held in Edmonton. However, I regret that the government neglected to consult the provinces and failed to secure beforehand the agreement of those provinces which already operate loteries. And that is why I suggest that Loto Canada should stop existing after 1979 and that Ottawa should afterwards return that jurisdiction to the provinces.
So in this area the federal government recognizes belatedly, one must admit, the national nature of the Olympic Games and agrees now with the official opposition which has always called for the active participation of Ottawa in the carrying out of an undertaking it had morally backed up with the International Committee as was the case when Montreal requested the Games. But Loto Canada must not be-a new source of division between Ottawa and the provinces nor between the citizens of the various regions of this country.
Incidentally, Mr. Speaker, in view of certain recently reported abuses by unconsciencious distributors one may wonder whether public authorities would not be well inspired to put the organization for the distribution and sale of tickets in the hands of some voluntary associations, and I am thinking of the veterans, the blind and the handicapped. The profits derived therefrom could be used to further the purposes of those associations even if they
June 3, 1976

should give the sellers a commission. Those additional funds would help those organizations to alleviate the financial burden imposed upon them through the assistance they provide to the more needy of their members.
Finally, and this is how I want to conclude my remarks, Mr. Speaker, the budget speech on May 25 will-have air impact abroad where, as is the case at home, the competence of this government is unreliable. Already suspected of being halfhearted with the Atlantic Alliance this government must now after the ridiculous Orion adventure restore its credibility with our allies. Let us also hope that we will not see another equally aberrant comedy when it comes to obtaining Leopard tanks.
The minister did not talk much about the major issues that remain undetermined between Canada and the United States, namely with respect to the Auto Pact and the irritants about which U.S. authorities are complaining. We are not much more informed about the nature of the discussion we have had with the Common Market and the importance of the barriers which up to now delayed the establishment of a contractual link between Canada and the European Economic Community.
Mr. Speaker, the same kind of silence persists about the negotiations entered into in the Tokyo Round and in which, however, the interests of our exporting industries are deeply involved. We are also completely in the dark about the specific projects of the government as regards the important problem which the conscience of the western world has to solve: that of the economic and food assistance to the underdeveloped countries whose inhabitants suffer from hunger. The news we had from Nairobi are far from being satisfactory. I hope we will soon know the position of the cabinet on all the questions which have been studied but which are far from being solved.
Either by bilateral or multilateral agreements, our country which, in spite of its present difficulties, is one of the most privileged in the world, must significantly increase its help to the millions of people who are without bread and who lack the minimal material comfort. Our generosity must be consistent with the hopes which the underdeveloped and underfed people have in us. If it is necessary, we must take ourselves the initiative of launching a new collective effort of the industrialized countries to this aim. Mr. Speaker, this is the price of international peace.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I say, since that occasion when we tabled the strategy, a number of very important measures have been taken to support the main thrust, the priority areas enunciated and outlined in that strategy paper. First, we have announced a new set of oil and natural gas prices for Canada fully consistent with the strategy. Second, my colleague the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Buchanan), and I tabled a policy statement that clarifies the terms and conditions under which the petroleum industry will operate on Canada lands-terms and conditions that will increase the exploration effort, increase our resource information and increase Canadian content and participation in the development of Canada's energy resources.
Last week, my colleague, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald), in his budget, announced a series of further initiatives that this government is taking to further our objectives of energy self-reliance. These are very important measures which fully support and reinforce those to 
which I have already alluded. There are three particular aspects of those energy measures in the budget which I should like to identify for hon. members of this House and particularly, perhaps, the opposition. The first is the further stimulus to exploration. The second is the economic incentives for the substitution of alternative energy sources for oil. The third is provision to further enhance the energy conservation proposals I have already announced, particularly in so far as they affect the use of motor gasoline.
For the exploration of alternate sources of oil and conservation there is a series of measures in each one of these policy priority areas. I believe these budget measures reinforce the basic thrust of the government's resource policy. They will enhance our ability to meet the specific energy targets and objectives in respect of energy self-reliance. In assessing the energy related budget measures, it is necessary to consider them in the context of both the government's energy policies as they are continuing to evolve, and the current and prospective economic situation. As the budget speech makes clear, we are embarked on an economic recovery in Canada, but the policy course we must steer is a very sensitive one if we are to move the Canadian economy back to its potential growth rate in a sure and steady way. Inappropriate action at this stage would inevitably lead to problems farther down the road. The greatest of these problems is the possibility that inflationary expectations could lead to a renewed outbreak of cost and price pressures that would abort the economic recovery in Canada and that would lead ultimately to declines in real purchasing power, curtailments in production and increased unemployment.
At the same time as our short-term economic situation demands careful monitoring and prudent management, it is obvious that a number of structural changes in our economic system are necessary if we are to be able to realize our potential over the longer term. Nowhere is this more apparent than with regard to our energy situation. We need to move domestic prices to a level that adequately reflects the higher costs of finding and producing new energy supplies in Canada. We need to encourage and stimulate more efficient methods of producing, distributing and using energy. We need to facilitate the reallocation of manpower, equipment and financial capital that will be required to augment our domestic energy supplies and enhance our self-reliance. We need, as well, to move deliberately and in an orderly way.
The necessary adjustments that producers and consumers of energy must make will have to be phased in an appropriate manner. Attempts to move too rapidly to develop crash programs that do not take account of the realities of the Canadian situation will waste scarce resources and lead to distortions and bottlenecks that will endanger our anti-inflation objectives and our prospects for real economic growth and employment.
The pricing decisions I announced for crude oil and natural gas reflect the manner in which these considerations must be balanced. Crude oil and natural gas were specifically exempted-I emphasize this-from the antiinflation program because it was recognized that upward relative price adjustments for these energy sources are essential. That is a point which not all members opposite
June 3, 1976

seem to realize, or perhaps some members opposite have short memories in this regard. At the same time, in determining the actual increases that should be permitted, the government would be acting irresponsibly if it did not consider the state of the economy at the time.
The first portion of the increase I announced for crude oil prices will lead to increases of about 3 cents per gallon in the price of motor gasoline and other petroleum products, including home heating oil. These price increases will take effect 60 days after July 1 of this year. In addition, the price of natural gas in residential use can be expected to increase by about 7.2 per cent, although the timing and exact magnitude of this increase will be determined by provincial regulatory agencies. Through the balance of 1976, these higher prices will increase the CPI by less than one percentage point. They will not unduly impair the success of the government's anti-inflation program, nor will they threaten the recovery that we foresee for the Canadian economy.
Further increases will occur in the spring of 1977, amounting to about 2 cents per gallon in the price of motor gasoline and other petroleum products, and 4.3 per cent for natural gas for residential consumers. These increases will have further inflationary impacts, but we are confident that by that time the anti-inflation program will have reduced inflationary expectations enough, and the economy will be sufficiently resilient, to allow these further increases to be absorbed in a smooth and orderly way.
Let me reiterate, again, that while the steps we take are tempered by current economic considerations, there should be no doubt as to the directions in which we are going. Those Canadians making investment decisions now, both consumers and producers, would be well advised to make those decisions on the basis of more expensive energy in the future. With these remarks as background, Mr. Speaker, let me turn specifically to the budget measures as they affect exploration activities and energy conservation initiatives. There are a number of changes in the budget that will further increase the incentives to explore and develop that currently exist in the federal tax structure. All payments made to acquire Canadian resource properties after May 6, 1974, will be included as part of development expenses; provincial incentives for exploration and development drilling will not be included in income; to the degree that provincial governments reimburse industry for federal taxes collected in respect of provincial royalties, these reimbursements will not themselves be subject to federal tax; and the depreciation allowance for offshore drilling platforms has been doubled, from 15 per cent to 30 per cent.
These measures will increase the cash flow to the petroleum industry in Canada and will further enhance the already considerable incentives to exploration that exist in the federal tax system. In addition, the suspension of the principal business test for a three-year period will allow those individuals and corporations who choose to invest in exploration, even though this is not their principal business, to expense their investments immediately. This will increase the ability of the petroleum industry to attract the capital and Canadian equity that is required for the exploration that must be undertaken if we are to assess
The Budget-Mr. Gillespie
adequately the options that are available to meet our future energy requirements.

Mr. Speaker, I believe there has been very limited attention so far in the press, and very little appreciation so far as the potential of that particular measure-the measure of removing the principal business tax. I believe it could have, potentially, a very important impact on new exploration activities in Canada, particularly from the point of view of the Canadian investor who has not always had an opportunity to invest. As a result of the new regulations I have referred to, the Canadian investor will have more opportunity and it will put him on a more equal basis with foreign investors who have been investing in our resources.
Hon. members will recall that the federal government's share of total production profits accruing to the petroleum industry in Canada is in the order of 17 per cent. As well as taxing at a relatively low rate, the federal system is highly sensitive to reinvestment. If, for example, producers reinvest about half of the $1.05 increase in the price of petroleum that will occur on July 1, the federal share of the incremental revenues will decrease from 27 per cent to 3 per cent. What this means, in very simple terms, is that about 50 per cent of new exploration investments can be financed with money that would otherwise have gone to the federal government in the form of taxes.
Let there be no mistake about this, Mr. Speaker. I am getting a little tired of reading the comments of critics within the industry, and outside, who claim that the federal government is taking a major share of the increase in price. Quite clearly, as I have already indicated this afternoon, the federal government will back off to a very small percentage if the additional price increase is reinvested in exploration. Indeed, if 57 cents of that dollar is reinvested in exploration in Canada, there will be no federal tax on that incremental increase.
Three cents.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Nothing for the federal government at all. In other words, the federal government backs right off to provide this degree of incentive. Some critics of the energy strategy we have adopted have suggested that our emphasis on exploration amounts to "putting all our eggs in one basket". It has been suggested that we are relying on frontier resources that, in the event, may not be there. This simply is not true. As I have pointed out on many occasions, there are a number of energy options available to us. But in order to know what we should do, we have first to know what we can do. And it is this need to know that makes accelerated exploration activity critical over the next three to four years. As I indicated previously, the federal government-through the existing fiscal system and the modifications announced in the budget-is contributing indirectly, but substantially, to exploration activity. We are also making a major, direct contribution through Petro-Canada. Hon. members will recall, I am sure, that the exploration budget for Petro-Canada this year will be $100 million, which will place it out in the forefront of companies exploring on Canadian lands. It is

June 3, 1976
The Budget-Mr. Gillespie
perhaps number one. Yet we still hear from the Tories opposite that they are against Petro-Canada.
What has it done for us yet? It has not done a thing. It is $700 million down the drain.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
I would hope that the producing provinces, who currently receive over 40 per cent of the production profits accruing to the petroleum industry, will assess the degree to which their incentive programs are appropriate in the context of our national objective of energy self-reliance.
The budget also introduces a number of measures that are supportive of our efforts to encourage the substitution of domestic energy sources for imported oil and to facilitate the introduction of renewable energy technologies. The extension of the two-year write-off of new capital equipment to equipment that can be used to produce energy from industrial and municipal wastes is an important measure in this regard. Many European countries, such as Germany and Sweden, generate a substantial proportion of their electrical energy from waste material, such as wood wastes produced in the lumber industry, or waste steam produced in a manufacturing industry. In Germany, this production is as high as 28 per cent of the total electrical capacity of the country. Preliminary estimates suggest that we might ultimately be able to supply 20 per cent of our electrical energy requirements from these sources. Thus, the budget measures should encourage the industrial sector to use energy resources more efficiently and encourage a diversity of electricity supply which will enhance the security of our national electrical supplies. Similarly, the removal of federal sales tax from items such as heat pumps, solar furnaces and heating panels, and wind-powered generating equipment will increase the commercial practicability of these alternative energy sources.
The final item in the budget which I want to address is the revisions to the excise taxes on heavy automobiles. While there are some variations, studies indicate that on average there is a close correlation between automobile weight and fuel consumption. Therefore, the increased excise taxes will reinforce the mileage standards I announced in February and are to be phased in over the same period as the mileage targets. Quite frankly, Mr. Speaker, I find myself puzzled by the reaction of the Canadian automobile industry to these tax increases. Some of the comments I have heard suggest that the taxes will not make any difference in consumer purchasing decisions. It is alleged that people will continue to demand heavy cars and will pay the higher price. At the same time, and sometimes from the same sources, it is suggested that the tax will lead to disruption in the automobile industry and to increased unemployment. Clearly, the industry's early reaction is a confusing one-it is not a well thought-out or consistent one.
I think it has been further confused by allegations that the government has arbitrarily forced the automobile companies to increase the weight of automobiles by 650 pounds for pollution and safety devices. On examining this, I find that roughly 50 additional pounds have been added for catalytic converters, and close to 600 pounds for safety reasons. I think it is fair to suggest to automobile manufac-
(Mr. Gillespie.]
turers that if 600 pounds are needed for safety reasons, there has to be something wrong with the kind of cars offered to the Canadian public in the past. The second point is that I believe it is fully within the capacity of the automobile industry to reduce the weight of the modern automobile through the substitution of materials without in any way effecting its safety. I have every reason to believe that some quite substantial reductions can, and will, be made by them in the near future.
We believe that Canadians will respond to the excise tax by demanding lighter, more energy-efficient cars. We also believe that the automobile industry in Canada is imaginative and responsive enough that those demands can, and will, be satisfied. There will undoubtedly be a period of adjustment in the industry, and it is precisely to make that adjustment as easy as possible that the tax provisions are being phased in over a four-year period.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I want to reiterate the theme with which I began. Adjusting to the realities of our energy situation will take time, and the adjustments must be made in a manner and at a pace that safeguards our economic objectives over the shorter term.
It is imperative, in this process, that consumers and producers know what the energy objectives of the government are so that they can plan accordingly. The publication of "An Energy Strategy for Canada", supported by the recent announcements with regard to domestic pricing and land and lease regulations, and further reinforced by the measures announced in the budget, make the directions of our energy policy clear and, more than that, the commitment of the federal government to these targets and priorities.

Mr. Speaker, we have just listened to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie), who usually gives a fairly constructive, straightforward speech; but today he was a great disappointment because he started off on a negative pitch and continued on a negative pitch all the way through. For some reason, he found it necessary to criticize the very excellent and constructive speech given by the hon. member for Sainte-Hyacinthe (Mr. Wagner). He said it was a disappointment, and then went on to castigate the hon. member for not talking about energy.
Then the minister proceeded for the next 20 or 25 minutes to bore the House to death with a rehash of what we have already heard in the budget, and told us absolutely nothing new. He spoke in glowing terms of a paper he had produced a short while ago called, as he put it, "An Energy Strategy for Canada," which is a very imposing title for something which could have been far better entitled, "Much Ado about Nothing"-because that policy paper really was a bust. It told us nothing about energy conservation which we did not already know, and announced no new plans, or workable plans, on the part of the government for conserving energy.
Then the minister talked about the energy price increases of a short time ago and how these are going to induce much greater exploration for oil and gas. But, as pointed out to the minister a couple of weeks ago in a
June 3, 1976

question at the beginning of the day, there is nothing in these price increases which have been granted to the oil companies which requires them to use this money for exploration. As I pointed out to the minister, these increases can be used in any one of three ways. They can be used to increase exploration, which is what is desired; but they can also be put into the company's reserves, or they can be paid out in additional dividends to shareholders. There is nothing to require the companies to do what the Canadian people and the government want them to do, and that is to increase their exploration activity. So we see the energy consumers of Canada subjected to a very real possibility that a great deal of the increase they are going to pay at the gas pump or in their bills for heating oil during the year is going to pay out fatter dividend cheques to shareholders in oil and gas companies.
There is nothing the government can do about it whatsoever, because there is no requirement of the oil companies that the money they get-the many millions of dollars they will get-in increased oil and gas prices should go into exploration. That is just another typical policy of this government which is badly thought-out and put through in a slipshod fashion.
I can just see the oil and gas company presidents gathering around the minister's office and telling the minister that he can count on them because they are his friends; that he can give them those prices and they will surely explore more. Then they will go out slapping their thighs and laughing themselves to death, saying that the minister is a poor old sucker and that he went for it again, the way John Turner did when he effected great increases by reductions in taxes about three years ago to increase productivity and industrial activity. The manufacturers and producers of this country told John Turner he could count on them and that they would increase productivity and plant and equipment, and they laughed all the way to the bank and did whatever they darned well pleased with the money the government gave to them by reducing their taxes.
The minister and the House know very well that that has not brought about anything like the results the then minister of finance assured the House those reductions would bring about. Unemployment was supposed to be lowered as a result of those gifts, but it has gone up steadily ever since, and those same producers and manufacturers, like the oil companies, are still laughing all the way to the bank. That is the kind of thing which is going on in this government, and unfortunately there is nothing we can do about it for the next two years. However, I can tell the government that in two years we are going to do a great deal about it, because we will move from this side of the aisle over to the other side and give this country the kind of government it deserves.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: Tell us what you are for, George.

I want, now, to say a few words in a quiet and modest way about the government's anti-inflation program and to put forward some concrete suggestions on my own behalf as to what I think the government should do to improve greatly the situation. Now that the anti-inflation program is approaching the end of its first year of operation, people are naturally asking two questions: What
The Budget-Mr. Hees
results have been achieved; and how long will it be necessary to keep it in operation? In answer to the first question, the inflation figures speak for themselves. During 1975, the consumer price index rose by 10.5 per cent. During the most recent 12-month period, the index went up by 9 per cent. Such results should be described, I think, as slow progress.
Regarding the second question: How long must controls remain in force?-the answer is a great deal more difficult to find. I do not think anybody really likes controls, and most people would like to get rid of them as soon as possible. But to answer the question: When can they be abandoned?, we will first have to look at the two reasons it was necessary to apply controls in the first place. The first reason was that the rapid and accelerating yearly increase in the consumer price index, commonly referred to as the cost of living, had driven prices to such a level that the average Canadian simply could not make his or her earnings keep up with the bills he or she had to pay.
As I have said, the cost of living went up by more than 10 per cent in 1975. This was not much of a problem for those whose yearly incomes were kept abreast of the cost of living by means of management or union contracts which increased as the cost of living increased. But the great majority of Canadians do not have such contracts, and they were suffering badly. This majority demanded that the government do something to control the cost of living and bring it back to a yearly increase which they could keep up with; and so controls were announced on October 13.
To find out what is a reasonable yearly increase in the consumer price index, we should look back over the yearly records of this indicator during the past 70 years, since it first began being recorded. During those 70 years, the average yearly increase was just under 3 per cent a year. Such an increase we found we could live with, and having found that we were able to keep our average yearly increases in expenditures-our inflation-to that level, people generally believed that we must make every possible effort to reduce our present inflation rate to that level once again, and keep it there.
The second reason for applying controls was that rapidly accelerating inflation was making our products less and less competitive in both the Canadian and the export market, and production and employment were adversely affected. In this regard, we are particularly vulnerable to price levels in the United States, the country which is by far our most important trading partner and with whom we do 70 per cent of our export and import trade. Neither Americans nor Canadians are willing to pay more for a Canadian product if they can buy a similar American product at a lower price. For many months now, the rate of inflation in the United States has been considerably lower than ours, and that is one of the reasons their economic recovery has been moving forward at a steadily accelerating pace and ours has not. Today, their rate of inflation is 6 per cent a year, while ours is 9 per cent. Moreover, in April the American secretary of the treasury, Mr. Simon, said that he is confident the United States will reach an inflation rate of 2 per cent within two years, which is April, 1978. Our government is aiming at 4 per cent by the end of 1978.
14124

June 3, 1976
The Budget-Mr. Hees
I think it is obvious that if we are to compete successfully with American products in the Canadian and United States markets and in the world market as well, we must achieve a rate of inflation roughly equal to theirs. To do so, we must accelerate our efforts very considerably. To achieve this, certain improvements must be brought about in the government's approach to reducing inflation. First of all, the government must reduce the rate of increase of the money supply-the total of bank deposits and cash in circulation-to a range far below the more than 10 per cent yearly rate at which the Bank of Canada is increasing the money supply today. The United States government has reduced its yearly rate of increase of MI to a range of between 4.5 per cent and 7 per cent, and that is the basic reason why they have been able to deal with inflation so much more successfully than we have. I believe that the Canadian government must strive to reach a comparable range within the next 12 months, a pace far quicker than they are moving today.
Second, I believe that the government must keep the increase in government spending each year to the increase targets which it has set for itself and for all Canadians. As you know, that target for the present year is 13 per cent, made up of 8 per cent, the estimated inflation for the present year, plus 5 per cent, the estimated growth in real domestic product for the year, for a total of 13 per cent. The government's present increase of 16 per cent above last year must be reduced to this figure as soon as possible. Finally, we must greatly increase our industrial productivity because of its very great effect on costs and selling prices.
Industrial productivity, expressed in terms of volume of production per man-hour, has been measured and recorded on a national basis in this country for the past 30 years. During that period, the average yearly increase has been 3.2 per cent, due to improved methods of production and new and improved plant and machinery. With yearly increases in productivity of around 3 per cent a year, we were able to keep our costs of production to a level where our selling prices were competitive with those of our principal industrial competitors in both the Canadian and export market, and unemployment and inflation remained at reasonable levels.
Then, four years ago, our yearly increase in industrial productivity began to decline. Whereas in 1971 we had shown an increase of 3 per cent over the previous year, in 1972 the increase over 1971 was only 2.6 per cent; in 1973, the increase over 1972 was only 1.5 per cent; in 1974, we showed an actual decrease of .5 per cent from 1973 and, in 1975, a decrease of 2.4 per cent from 1974.
These accelerating decreases in industrial productivity have caused costs and selling prices to rise sharply, contributing heavily to inflation. They have also brought about higher unemployment, because people in this country and abroad will not pay more for a Canadian product if they can buy a similar product made in some other country for less money, and Canadian production has suffered as a result of this falling demand.
What has contributed greatly to our difficulties in finding customers who will pay the prices we are asking is the fact that United States industrial productivity has been
rising as rapidly as ours has been falling. The result has been that we have been losing sales to United States producers at a steadily accelerating rate. It is obvious that we must introduce measures to increase industrial productivity, so that we can bring inflation back to a yearly increase roughly comparable to that of the United States and thereby make our selling prices competitive with those of our principal competitor. To do so, we must offer incentives which will persuade producers they will be able to pay for the new plant, machinery and production systems they will have to buy in a reasonably short space of time and, in this way, make it as easy as possible for them to make the usually high expenditures involved in the kinds of purchases I outlined.
The kinds of incentives I have in mind would be the following: First, all capital expenditures would be written off in two years. Second, a plant would be rewarded in the form of a generous cash bonus at the end of the year, in proportion to its increase in productivity during the year, compared to the base year-the last full year before the plan goes into operation. This form of incentive has been very effective in increasing productivity in such countries as Japan and West Germany, where spectacular results have been achieved since the end of the Second World War. There is no reason why such an incentive would be less successful in this country today.
So I think that the answer to our original question, when can controls be ended, is that the people of Canada will not agree to their removal until inflation is lowered to a level where they have found in the past that it can be tolerated, at around 3 per cent a year. Also, I do not believe that we can relax our efforts until we bring inflation to a level where we can once again compete successfully with our principal economic competitor, the United States, for the Canadian, the United States and the world market. That level will also be no more than 1 per cent above the United States target of 2 per cent a year, or no more than 3 per cent. In other words the answer to the question, when can controls be ended, is not a matter of time but of performance and results. The task before the government and the Canadian people is a formidable one, but one which must be tackled without delay. Reluctance to tackle the task vigorously will be very serious for the welfare of this country.
Now let us take a look at which direction the economy should take after controls have been discontinued. Once the target of 3 per cent inflation has been reached, I think it is obvious that it must be kept within that range for the good of the economy and for the good of the Canadian people. If there is a significant move by those elements of society whose pressures caused inflation to rise rapidly during the past few years to start it on another upward spiral, then controls will, of course, have to be reimposed. If we are to avoid having to reimpose controls, it must be made crystal clear that that will be done if those elements of our economy which have it within their power to create excessive inflation are unwilling to control their actions for the general good of the country.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I believe that if it is made very clear and definite that this country has no intention of going through another round of spiralling inflation, once the present inflation has been brought within reasonable
(Mr. Hees.
June 3, 1976

bounds, we will have a very good chance of proceeding with a prosperous economy, free of the kinds of controls which were imposed last October.

Mr. Speaker, the first budget presented by the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) was characterized by the Financial Post writer, George Radwanski, who is certainly not a flaming radical, as a-
-continuation of a trend toward a nasty, gutless kind of conservatism-
Anyone who studies the budget will agree with Mr. Radwanski. The budget of this minister of finance shows the truth of the old adage-the more things change, the more they remain the same. Former ministers of finance, Mr. Benson and Mr. Turner, are gone. They are relatively silent. The former deputy minister of finance, Mr. Reis-man, is gone but is still vocal. However, the effect of this budget will be the effect of budgets which they presented in recent years.
Those budgets produced hardships on the ordinary citizen of this country. This budget will do the same. They produced more unemployment. I predict that a year from now there will be an additional 100,000 on top of the present 760,000 unemployed at the present time. That is based on the best economic advice we have been able to get from economists who have been much more accurate in their predictions in recent years than economists of the Department of Finance.
The minister spoke glowingly and proudly about the way that inflation has slowed down in the past three or four months. I suggest that he dampen his enthusiasm. It is obvious to almost every business analyst and economist, other than the trained seals who work for the government, that the slowdown has been, and will be, very temporary. The slowdown in the rate of inflation was almost exclusively as a result of a reduction in food prices. Mrs. Plump-tre of the late and unlamented Food Prices Review Board, now of the Anti-Inflation Board, agrees that food prices are going up.
There have been sharp increases in provincial and municipal taxes. They increased as a result of cutbacks forced on the provinces by the federal government. For the two largest provinces in particular, Ontario and Quebec, this has been a mean and regressive increase and has resulted in a doubling of hospital and medical insurance premiums. The increased cost to every family will be between $50 and $100 per year.
The federal government has agreed to increases in the price of oil and gas. Oil will increase $1.05 a barrel on July 1, and another 70 cents a barrel on January 1, 1977. That represents an increase of 5 cents a gallon in the wholesale price. Retailers will probably add on their increases. Therefore, every person who buys gas for his car or oil to heat his house will be affected. The price of natural gas has also been increased. For those families using natural gas, their costs will increase next winter between $40 and $50 for the heating season.
Last year, the increase in the cost of living was 10V2 per cent. Although for the past three or four months it has
The Budget-Mr. Orlikow
been going up at a slower rate, it will go up more quickly beginning in July. From July to the end of the year there will be an increase of about 1 per cent per month. By the end of 1976, the increase in the cost of living will be 9 per cent as compared with the 10V2 per cent increase in 1975. As if that were not bad enough, there will be a substantial increase in the rate of unemployment. In his budget speech, the minister stated that government estimates are that there will be an increase in the number of jobs in Canada of 250,000. However, the number of people who will be looking for work will increase by about 350,000.
Unemployment has been rising steadily. Last month, calculated on the seasonally adjusted basis, it was 7.4 per cent. That was the highest rate of unemployment in Canada since 1961. On the basis of any estimates one wants to make, it is obvious that this winter the unemployment rate, on a seasonally adjusted basis, will not be 7 per cent but 8 per cent. That is a tragedy for this country as a whole. However, it is sheer disaster for the slow growth areas.
Last month, the national rate of unemployment was 7.4 per cent. However, in Newfoundland there was 16.3 per cent unemployment. On the northeast coast of Labrador the unemployment rate was 19.8 per cent. In New Brunswick the rate was 13.2 per cent, and in the northeast part of that province, 26.3 per cent. Under those circumstances, is it any wonder that the members of this party object so strenuously to the proposal in the budget, and elaborated on yesterday by the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras), that the period which people must work before qualifying for unemployment insurance will be increased from 8 to 12 weeks?
When the Minister of Finance made his budget address some days ago there were cries of protest, not just from members of this party but from Liberal members from Newfoundland and Conservative members from New Brunswick and Newfoundland. Yesterday, our amendment objecting to the increased qualifying period was voted on. It was an amazing sight. All the protesters, led by the minister who introduced the unemployment insurance legislation in 1971, the present Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Mackasey), were absent from the House and did not have to vote against the amendment. That was true of Liberal and Conservative members from the slow-growth areas.
The minister and some members of the House may think that we are being partisan for protesting that infamous proposal of the government. Let us see what the provincial governments whose people will be most adversely affected have to say. I quote from the Toronto Star of Friday, May 28:
Finance Minister A. E. Stairs of New Brunswick said the extension of the period of eligibility and the changes in the length of benefit "clearly indicate a substantial shift in the burden of social assistance to the province from the federal government."
He said, also:
It is most unfortunate that this kind of program change should be made without extensive prior analysis of the impact on regions such as ours.
95568-60^

June 3, 1976
The Budget-Mr. Orlikow
Then the Nova Scotia minister of labour, a Liberal, Mr. Walter Fitzgerald, said he was discouraged by the proposals. A recent provincial study estimated that 14,800 people would lose their benefits of more than $9 million, he said. In pockets where unemployment was highest, such as Sydney, the net loss of direct income was predicted to be $3.3 million. That is what the ministers from the provinces with the highest unemployment are saying. For the Minister of Manpower and Immigration to say, as he did yesterday, that there would not be much hardship, that most of the people concerned could extend their period of work from 8 weeks to 12 weeks, and thus qualify, is to cast a slur on the bulk of the people who are unemployed and drawing benefits. The minister is implying that people work for eight weeks and then quit voluntarily so that they can draw unemployment benefits. Except when the minister has to make excuses, as was the case yesterday, he knows better.
When we talk about a rate of 7.4 per cent unemployment nationally, we are excluding native people almost entirely because native people who live on reserves are not counted when compiling the national rate. The minister should know this as well as I do, because there are a large number of native people in his constituency. He knows it, the Minister of Finance knows it, and I know it-but it is very likely that people in general do not. As I say, we have knowingly, and in a calculated manner, excluded the native people. The fact is, as the minister is aware, that between 60 per cent and 80 per cent of the native people who live on reserves are unemployed for all or part of the year. They are not even counted by those who compile the unemployment figures.
The minister implied yesterday that the government still believes in full employment. Here is what he said, and members can find his words at page 14085 of yesterday's Hansard:
Our goal is not necessarily a 5 Vi per cent or even a 5 per cent unemployment rate. Our goal is the lowest employment rate possible having regard to inflationary pressures and the economic situation.
What the minister did not say was that his goal is somewhere between a rate of 7 per cent and 8 per cent. Liberal cabinet ministers always pay lip service to the idea of full employment. When the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs was introducing amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act in 1971, he said:
I imagine somebody is going to suggest that the government has determined 4 per cent to be an acceptable rate of unemployment in Canada. Well, it is not my criterion. Like everybody else, I believe the acceptable rate is the lowest possible rate.
He was saying that 4 per cent is too high. Now the Minister of Manpower and the Minister of Finance, are regarding a rate of more than 7 per cent as being acceptable to them. In the course of a CBC broadcast on January 9, 1972, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said:
We have already entered into better times. I think the prodding will be less perhaps in the economic sphere; you won't be worried; you know you'll have 96 per cent of the work force employed .. . your concerns will be oriented more and more to the 96 per cent or 95 per cent of the population which is working and secure.
So, in 1972 the Prime Minister was accepting 4 per cent as being adequate. Now we are close to 7.5 per cent, with the rate likely to go up, and the government is not concerned at all. We are sometimes told by both Liberals and
Conservatives that whether the rate of 7.4 per cent or 4 per cent, as it was a few years ago, the figures are misleading because there are lots of people who could find work at any time if they chose to do so.
Some members say that anyone who wants a job can get one. Mr. Speaker, the facts prove the contrary. At a time when there are more than 750,000 unemployed, the number of job vacancies is down substantially as compared with last year, especially in areas of high unemployment like Newfoundland. Job vacancies in the first quarter of 1975 amounted to 61,000 in all of Canada; in the first quarter of 1976 there were 48,100. In Newfoundland there were just 500 job vacancies, and in that province, as I have stated, 13 per cent of the work force is unemployed. So there is no way in which unemployed people in Newfoundland can get jobs at the present time. There were 15,400 job vacancies in Ontario, and I believe there were six times that number of unemployed in the province. So we face a situation of large-scale unemployment created by government policies. And who will bear the brunt? The unemployed and the people who work. The unemployed, because they will be cut off from benefit if they have not worked 12 weeks, and the employed who will have to pay higher premiums to make up for the deficit in the unemployment insurance fund.
We are seeing a two-step retreat from the financial commitment of the Liberal party in 1971 to create jobs for the unemployed. The 1971 act provided that the federal government would pay the cost of all extended benefits and the total cost of all benefits payable when unemployment rose above 8 per cent. According to the minister at that time, this provided an incentive for the government to keep unemployment down and thus restrict the size of the pay-out. In December, 1975, Bill C-69 amended the scheme so as to change the federal government's commitment from one based on the straight 4 per cent level to one based on an eight-year moving average. In effect, federal contributions kick in much later, as a result-in 1976 at 5.6 per cent, to be precise.
Amendments are now being proposed in the budget to reduce the financial obligation of the federal government still further by lowering the contributions payable when unemployment exceeds 4 per cent. We can understand why the Liberal minister of social services in Nova Scotia said at the opening of the meetings where the premiers rejected the welfare proposals of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde):
If the federal government keeps escalating the price of oil and tightening unemployment insurance, we're going to have the whole province on social assistance.
This is the sort of thing that has happened with a government led by a "mod" Prime Minister, a modern guy who has the media all agog. He knows what the people are interested in and can anticipate their wants. He can move to meet their needs. What he has done in fact, as I have indicated, is not only to give us the highest unemployment we have had in 15 years, but he has tried to convince the people of Canada that they should accept this as normal and as the right way to do things.
Let me compare for a moment this "mod" Prime Minister, who is really "with it", as our young people say, with

June 3, 1976

an old-fashioned, liberal political leader in the United States, a man who has been in politics for a long time, who is presently a senator and was once vice-president and a presidential candidate, failing to get elected by less than one per cent of the vote, Hubert Humphrey. We Canadians read American newspapers and magazines a great deal and we picture Hubert Humphrey as somehow old-fashioned, that he really is not "clued in" to the 1970s. I want to put on the record a few paragraphs from the Congressional Record printed in Washington for January 15, 1975. Senator Humphrey had introduced a bill, the equal opportunity and full employment act for 1975, and I would like hon. members to compare what Senator Humphrey proposed with the record of this "mod", up-to-date government which has permitted, indeed welcomed, 7.4 per cent unemployment. He said:
In December, 6.5 million Americans, 7.1 per cent of of the labour force, were "officially" counted as unemployed. Of course, for members of minority groups conditions were much worse.
In the last 12 months "official" unemployment among blacks rose 50 per cent, from 888,000 to 1.3 million people.
I pause there for a moment to suggest that if we compare our record for employing native people with the United States' record for employing black people, we Canadians would have to hang our heads in shame. Senator Humphrey went on to say this:
In 1948, the "right to work" was clearly established in the Universal Declaration of Human Rights adopted by the United Nations ...
Despite the official declarations and the generally well-intentioned policy pronouncements, we have failed dismally to provide "jobs for all". Large segments of our population, especially women, the young, the old, the poorly educated, and ethnic minorities, have had their "right to work" ignored and, in many cases, the fact of their unemployment swept under the rug and conveniently out of sight by "official" statistics.
... it is time to fulfil this promise of "jobs for all," a promise that far too long has gone unmet. We must guarantee an equal opportunity to work at fair wages to every person in our nation who is able and willing to work.
He then went on to outline how he proposed that this be done. He called for the establishment of local reservoirs of public service and private employment projects developed by local planning councils in co-operation with community job boards. He called for the creation of a job guarantee office able to fund public and private work projects developed through the local reservoirs. Senator Humphrey was not talking about some band-aid, cosmetic measures, like a few LIP or OFY projects; he was talking about jobs for everybody, about unemployment of probably of 2.5 to 3 per cent. That is not too far removed from the 4 per cent unemployment level which over the years the Economic Council has calculated would be full employment in this country.
We have argued that dealing with unemployment is the number one priority in this country. We have argued that to meet the threat of unemployment what we need is a budgetary deficit that is substantially greater than that proposed by the minister, so as to give the economy the stimulation it needs to get people back to work. Our calculations indicate that a deficit in the order of $4.5 billion would be necessary in order to inject any significant stimulus into the economy this year. This would mean a tax cut, preferably for those in the lower income brackets, of about $1.2 billion.
The Budget-Mr. Orlikow
In addition, we have argued that we should end the indexing of income tax and the assortment of middle-class tax gimmicks that the government has introduced in recent years. This would free another $1.5 billion that could be included in a redistributive tax cut. Such an amount, roughly $3 billion, would be enough to provide a sizeable tax cut, which we have calculated to be in the neighbourhood of $250 for each person who files a tax return that shows an income of $15,000 and under. It is our belief that these are people who essentially do not save money; they would spend this tax cut of $250 and the injection of this money would lead to the purchase of goods and services, which in turn would immediately bring about a sharp reduction in the number of people unemployed.
With 7.4 per cent unemployment, Mr. Speaker, the economy needs a stimulus in the order of the roughly $3 billion tax cut that I have mentioned. This is a doubly advantageous time to provide such a tax cut because the income redistributive effects of ending the middle-class tax gimmicks would provide more equity to the system at the same time as it was delivering increased income to the bottom end of the income scale, where it would tend to be spent rather than saved, as I have already said.
The only objection that we have heard to a tax cut at this time, an objection raised by the Minister of Finance, is that the stimulation of demand on the kind of scale I have suggested would rekindle inflation. We reject that opinion. We insist that that is not a valid argument, for the simple reason that all these statistics that have been released by Statistics Canada, the Department of Finance and the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce show very clearly that the industrial sector of our economy at the present time is operating at only about 80 per cent of capacity.
Although some of this has caused a slump in exports, a great deal of this excess capacity could be geared to domestic markets. We believe such a stimulation of the domestic market would not be inflationary but would lead to an economic recovery. It would use up our unused capacity, put people back to work, and in the long run have a positive effect on the rate of inflation. If you make housing more available and reduce the high cost of purchasing homes, the shortage and the high cost factor would tend to disappear. It seems to us, again-
