subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would especially like to thank you today for allowing me to join some of the elite of the political parties to present my first comments on the budget. I should also like to commend the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) for presenting a most realistic budget. In these inflationary times this is the kind of budget that is needed. It is the kind of budget that is going to be instrumental in combating the economic difficulties we are facing.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You can do better that that, Joe.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
If you will listen, it becomes even more succulent. It is the kind of budget that is going to be instrumental in combating this kind of difficulty. It is a realistic budget that does not suggest quick or facile methods. Nor does it entail draconian methods. Certain government critics may condemn the Minister of Finance for proceeding far too cautiously. I would think they should be reassured to know that their country's economic future is

being handled cautiously. This is not a time for magnificent extravaganzas; this is a time for restraint, for economic recovery and for reality.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Who wrote that-you Don?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
If hon. members will pay close attention they will realize this is a wallner research report and, therefore, is very special. I do not claim to be an economist, but I certainly do know that Canada's material prosperity is at stake. As was to be expected, the May 25 budget is inextricably linked to the anti-inflation program. Of the 1,500 largest Canadian companies that fall under the direct control of the Anti-Inflation Board, 35 have head offices in Kitchener, Waterloo, Cambridge, Guelph and Stratford. More than 40 others have head offices elsewhere but are major employers in this area, including such a local giant as Uniroyal Limited.
There are also many companies with local branch offices, distribution centres, franchise outlets or stores in the area. Among them are all the major banks, most of the major retail store chains, car dealerships, mortgage and insurance companies and service industries, such as those involving computers, office copying machines, etc. Naturally, the business community of the Kitchener area watched with interest the proceedings of Tuesday last.
The Minister of Finance reported in his budget speech that the controls program has begun to take effect. When the anti-inflation measures were introduced last October, the consumer price index was at 10.6 per cent and rising. By December it had dropped to below 10 per cent, and it dropped to 9.1 per cent in Feburary, the best record in well over two years. There has been excellent public support for the anti-inflation program. A public opinion poll showed that fully 61 per cent were in favour, while only 22 per cent were opposed. The May, 1976, budget is another measure which increases the whole effectiveness of the anti-inflation program. It is meant to enhance the steps taken in other areas, especially in respect of reductions in government spending and cutbacks in the growth of the public service.
A Kitchener chamber of commerce publication describes my constituency as being noted for its sausages, Schneider's sausages, its spareribs, its pigtails, its sauerkraut and its good food in general. But, it is also known for its television sets, its fine furniture, its electronic components, its shirts, its sweaters, its shoes, the stability of its labour, the high productivity of its workers, its hospitality and its reputation as a desirable community. The budget just presented will support and encourage this good life in Kitchener, Mr. Speaker.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I commend the hon. member who has just resumed his seat for the brevity which characterized his remarks. I have never pretended that I have been popular in all the years I have been here, but at least one claim I am able to make is that no Speaker has ever had to rise to tell me that the hon. member's time had expired. Perhaps that is because I have good eyesight and have seen the Speaker starting to rise, but I have always avoided that error.
Normally, it is a very ebullient pleasure for me to take part in the general debate on the throne speech and the
June 3, 1976

budget debate, especially when on occasions such as this afternoon I see around me a cro'wded, hushed and expectant House.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
This year and in this session, sir, I have lost some of that high excitement which usually characterizes my learned and deliberated utterances. I find this is not one of the parliamentary sessions which brings a great deal of uplift to me. I note, in beginning, in a very mundane way, that we have now reached over 14,000 pages- not words, but pages of Hansard. If anybody thinks that is not too long for a group of parliamentarians to be together talking about the same sorts of things, I disagree with that person. It is a time, also, when there is certainly unease about the management of our national affairs. We have a cabinet divided; we have resignations; we have near-resignations; we have a government seeking to put into effect an aborted form of policy or proposal the opposition to which brought it into office.
We have a society which is seriously divided. A major segment thereof, namely, labour, is strongly and seriously committed against a major aspect of the government's program. We have scandals; we have near-scandals; we have suggestions; we have anxiety. I may say that never in my now, fairly long time in public life and my much longer period of study of Canadian political institutions have I seen anything more reprehensible than the behaviour of the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Goyer) in the manner in which he tried publicly and in this place to thrust responsibility and blame upon a public servant. That, I thought, was a new low. We are becoming accustomed to in-fighting among ministers, to the absence of ministers and to the passing of blame from one minister to another; but I think most heinous and reprehensible is the attempt in public and in parliament to throw the arrow of responsibility and culpability on a senior public servant who has no chance to appear before us and state his case.
I also think, since this long session began, about what great changes have occurred. This does not mean I have a magnificent memory; however, I can remember when that most handsome man, that brilliant athlete, that gem in the French and English-speaking world, John Turner, was here. Where is he now? Where has he gone? In this long procession of history we began with Prince Charming. Then he was "Mr. Clean", "The man from Glad", "The architect of our economy". Where is he now? Why has he gone? Did the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Trudeau) think that the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Macdonald) was potentially a better minister of finance? Did he think he was a better architect of our nation's future in economic, monetary and fiscal terms?
I am quite capable of criticizing the Prime Minister, although I am not a partisan man. But I have never accused him of really believing that. That, I would not charge him with. So we are left with the greatest failure as House leader that any parliament has ever seen, and he is moving on in his great, lumbering gait to become the most disastrous minister of finance this country has ever seen.
The Budget-Mr. Macquarrie
In this budget debate it is not our task or my job to reflect upon the difficulties of the Prime Minister, although if I were totally relaxed I could enjoy some of these reflections. We must think about the state of the national economy. It is our job to analyse and assess the pertinent and pressing facts of our national economic life. What, sir, is happening to this country? What are the portents, and where is our present leadership leading us?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Onwards and ever upwards.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
He says, "Onwards and ever upwards," but my dear friend did not go upwards as he should have. If I were a cabinet-maker, I would have put him up. I am old enough in this parliamentary stage to remember when budget night was a great experience; the galleries were packed and the House was packed. We came here; we waited and we listened for portents, for forecasts, for policies and for analyses which were going to be important. We waited expectantly for those changes which would alter the life of the nation and affect the lives of all the people in the nation. Canadians waited expectantly for something which would have a bearing upon their day-today economic existence.
But what of May 25? After the great speech had been delivered, what was the result? In our highly-computerized and technological society, could even the most sensitive computer measure the degree of uplift among any sector of Canadian society? The most common, and perhaps the most frequent, description of the minister's effort was that euphemistic expression "stand-patism". Indeed, I wondered then, and I wonder still, why it was thought necessary to present a budget at all. Many thousands of seasonally employed Canadians will suffer; but apart from this group, what benefits will flow to the Canadian population; what will be the strengthening effect upon the sagging Canadian economy?
The question is almost a rhetorical one. The impressive, serious and compelling economic indices are all negative- indeed, profoundly disturbing. Before I came to this House, I spent many years studying what was called the dismal science, the study of economics. It was dismal then, and it is dreary now! But one thing we were taught by our professors was that inflation and unemployment were cyclical developments, one following the other and that if the economy was well managed, you would not have either.
It is the great achievement of this government-which has been in power for 13 years-that it has broken that law. The government has stood that law on its head or on its posterior-whichever it is-and we have inflation and unemployment together: not only together but, additionally, seemingly forever! Both inflation and unemployment are together and in the average month we see from Statistics Canada the same distressing statistics no matter how devious may be the effort to alter the formula.
Expressions like, "seasonally adjusted" are now ancient. About five years ago, someone asked me what it meant, and I said that I was not sure. However, I did say that I thought it meant that it is not as bad as it could be. I think I am right in that. In this twentieth century, with the very best efforts and with the greatest deficits, we have 7.4 per cent of our work force out of work. No matter how one describes it, that is far too many unemployed Canadians.

June 3, 1976
The Budget-Mr. Macquarrie
Not only is that continuing this month, but it has been continuing month after month since we converted into the "just" society.
We have a great army of functionaries. We have all sorts of people on the Anti-Inflation Board. If the Prime Minister could not wrestle inflation to the ground, who is to say that the callous Jean-Luc Pepin, or the more callous Mrs. Plumptre are doing the job. Of course we will not bring inflation to the ground. Any housewife or house spouse in Canada knows that. While it might seem economically sound to talk about stand-pattism on budget night, and while we may watch all the postures and expostulations of ministers and their apologists, we know that when that is all over there is not a single hopeful or positive sign to which they may point. Of course, they may hope that somehow in the United States things may get better and that we may benefit from the economic recovery in that country. I imagine when that day comes we will not receive any telegraphed messages from the Secretary of the Treasury of the United States. The ministers of this government will be taking credit, and not admitting it is just a spin-off from the American development.
My colleagues have discussed many aspects earlier in their fine discussions and argumentations and I know that further examinations of our national situation will follow. I want to pay tribute to my colleague, the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens), who has made an excellent analysis of our economy. I have the mildest, most subtle suggestion for the minister-he will not be there for more than 24 months at the most-in his disagreement with complete secrecy in the budget. If he wants to go out of office with some degree of credibility, I suggest he listen to our spokesman and others who have thought about these things very carefully and have put the national interest ahead of party advantage.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the first member from the Atlantic region who has spoken on this side, I want to focus my thoughts for a short while on the vital question of regional disparity. Coming from Atlantic Canada, I think that I have the right to draw upon my experience in this field. '
In the construction of a federal state, it is the very ethos of such a developing organization that the advantages and disadvantages of the component regions be recognized and shared. If the Atlantic area has suffered because of national policies, it is surely quite clearly and rightly and properly the responsibility of the national authorities to make redress, to make adjustment and to make equalization for that situation. The basic question in the discussions in Charlettown in 1864-a city which I have the honour to represent in this parliament-concerned the great economic questions affecting the various regions. As John A. Macdonald said more than once, 90 per cent of all the agreements were made at the Charlottetown meeting in September, 1864.
Since this is general debate, Mr. Speaker, I might say that in the present mild flurry of discussion about our constitution I hear the Prime Minister talk about the

patriation of our constitution. I should like to take the opportunity of saying to him that if it is necessary to use that non-word, at least he should recognize Canadian history and recall that the British North America Act, although entirely and technically an emanation of the British parliament, was in fact the product of Canadian discussions, of Canadian statemanship, and in every way was "made in Canada". So if we must use the Latin construction "patria", which is so dated, when we talk about patriotism-the word is not "patriation", but "repatriation"-we are bringing back to Canada that which was made in Canada by great and distinguished Canadian statesmen, the chief of whom was Sir John A. Macdonald.
To move from terminology to economics, Mr. Speaker, I must say that I am profoundly disturbed about what is happening in the Atlantic region. I have often said in this House that just because we have grown accustomed to national policies working to our disadvantage there is no reason why we should be asked to like those policies. Overexposure does not in this case mean overaffection and the purpose of this government-especially in relation to the Department of Regional Economic Expansion and most recently in the budget of May 25-brings little cheer to Atlantic Canada and the long-suffering people from that area where this nation began.
We still have month after month, year after year, the highest unemployment rate in the whole country. Our cost of living is still high; our wages are low! Month after month the grim statistics tell their tale. In those indices of prosperity which should be high, we are generally, universally and apparently eternally, low. In those areas where a low figure indicates economic well-being, we have these figures high. One has only to examine these statistics of unemployment. One has only to refer to the report on the cost of living, which gives the annual income of our people year after year after year, to check the veracity of the assertion I am making. Time after time I have tried to convince successive ministers of public works that it is a cruel injustice to pay people working for the government of Canada in the Atlantic region a lower per-hour rate than those doing the same work in the rest of Canada. The prevailing wage rate program is one of the greatest economic deterrents to maritime prosperity that I can think of.
I have said that the Department of Regional Economic Expansion is of immense importance to the sea-girt provinces of the east. It is the department which has special responsibilities for programs designed to redress some of the grave imbalances in our national economy. That is a good thing, and it is an important department. It is of the essence that regional economies be strong. No nation can be really prosperous or economically strong if any of its constituent parts are suffering from chronic economic depression. That is why 100 years ago Sir John A. Macdonald, after serious discussions with Joseph Howe, admitted quickly that changes in the basic document, the British North America Act, must be made to bring about a degree of justice to Nova Scotia and the Atlantic region. All these foolish announcements about special status for certain provinces being wrong is not historically true; all our provinces have special problems. Those whose economy has been damaged by national policies have all the more right to a special regard from the national government. I
June 3, 1976

believe all of us in this House from Atlantic Canada and all our people want DREE and the minister to be successful, to really accomplish something and to diminish the gulf of inequity which retards a healthy economy.
I congratulate the new minister. I have high regard for him and wish him well in all his endeavours. But I regret that we see indications of serious communication problems between his department and its provincial counterpart in Prince Edward Island. At least this is the view of the Hon. Gilbert Clements who appeared before the Standing Committee on Regional Development on May 23 and who had some sharp criticism of the federal department. He told the committee:
But I have no hesitation in saying that the communications with DREE and the action that we get from DREE is very poor . . .
The attempt to decentralize, as far as I am concerned personally as one minister, is not worth it. We have a bureaucratic bog that is very difficult to cut through, and I think this is where the whole problem is. You ask a simple question and it gets lost in the wheel. You just do not see it again. It is very difficult for my people in my department to be continually trying to get answers to very simple, basic questions while we have a lot of work to be done.
Later at the same meeting, Mr. Clements declared:
I can just answer this way. We are not the only province that is having problems with DREE, as I indicated, by the four ministers. Their frustrations are equally as great as mine. So there is nothing special about the plans in the other Atlantic provinces so it would look as though the problem is the same.
I do not object to dealing with all kinds of people in Moncton and Charlottetown at all, as long as the pipeline to whoever makes the answer is open. But when you get the pipeline clogged then you are in real trouble and, of course, if you are dealing direct with Ottawa and you get a plugged pipeline then you are no better off.
He went on to say:
But it seemed that under the first part of the plan when I was not really involved with it, the line to Ottawa was more direct, the answers were direct, and progress was made. Now it is difficult to even sit down and have a meeting with people. I was just indicating to your chairman here, a top level*person in our province requested a meeting with DREE a month and a half ago that has not taken place.
I suppose that it is not surprising that there should be problems between Mr. Clements and the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion in Prince Edward Island. The present government has been notable in the development of a climate of misunderstanding between the federal and provincial levels of jurisdiction. One recalls the recent and repeated pleas of Premier Regan on the energy problems of the province of Nova Scotia, and I recall the chastising lecture which was given by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie) which was recently replaced by a more reasonable attitude. The Premier of Prince Edward Island must feel eternally the odd man out, because his representations on transportation, national parks and other vital questions seem, if not unnoted, at least to be unheeded.
But much more serious than the lack of communication between the federal DREE minister and his provincial counterparts is the perpetual situation where it appears that no other minister in the federal cabinet communicates with the DREE minister. That department was set up, and rightly so, to look upon the inequalities between regions of Canada and to do all in the power of the national government to diminish the gulf between those economically
The Budget-Mr. Macquarrie
disadvantaged regions and the national average. That is a laudable and proper role for the national government, and it is one which only the national government can perform.
Former Premier Smith of Nova Scotia was constitutionally right and proper when he had that inserted on the agenda for the dominion-provincial conference-if I may use that proper and correct word "dominion"-but if none of the colleagues of the minister pay the slightest attention to this concept, we are not going to get very far. What is the use of having the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion assert and try to carry out the notion that there are special needs in certain areas of this country requiring special action by the national government, if his colleagues, one after another, say that they must apply a uniform standard?
Did the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) listen to his colleague, the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion, with reference to the ferry situation? Our great problem is to transport the products of the sea and the soil, to other parts, as well as tourists, and our Minister of Transport allowed a 100 per cent increase in one ferry rate and a 60 per cent increase in another. He enunciates the brilliant theory: let the user pay the fare. I will not begin to tell how many people in the Atlantic provinces pay for the St. Lawrence Seaway.
Did the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Buchanan) consult his colleague when he forced the people of Prince Edward Island to go to the beaches of the North Shore by entering the Prince Edward Island national park? In other words, until there is recognition by all the members of the cabinet that there are special factors affecting the disadvantaged regions, then the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion will never be able to make a success of his very important portfolio, and I am wondering if there is even yet a glimmer of recognition by the present government of the great problems facing the Atlantic region.
The only innovative idea I saw in the statement of the Minister of Finance of May 25-and I commend him for this-was the suggestion that something should be done for those who are moving to alternate power sources. I congratulate him for that. I cannot see anything else. I have not seen, for one moment, in the mind of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources the slightest recognition of the energy situation affecting the maritime provinces. It is easy for him to give little lectures to the provinces about cutting down their highway speed and turning off their lights-but he can watch, and if he is at all interested he can study the situation with reference to the Fundy tides. We all believe, or we say we do, that we are heading toward a future in which energy resources will be very seriously drained. There are few energy sources which are renewable; but in Atlantic Canada today we have a magnificent source of energy which, as long as the earth, the sun and the moon endure, will be there. That is longer than most of us will be here.
The Fundy tidal study has been analysed and researched in depth; studies have been made of the studies. We know it can be done. We all know that the time will come when it must be done; but did we see the slightest scintilla of suggestion in the budget the other night about this magnificent source of energy? I fear that if the present

June 3, 1976
The Budget-Mr. Kaplan
administrators of our realm are in possession of the keys of the kingdom for 24 more months, nothing will be done and there will be a delay until we reach the stage where it has to be done-and the cost will be many times greater than it would be now. I believe it was the great French philosopher, Montesquieu, who said: "To govern is to foresee". Heaven help us! We have tried and tried to help the present government foresee the energy needs of the whole country and the energy opportunities in the Atlantic provinces.
I listened carefully to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras) when he had the placatory job of picking up the broken pieces from the crumbling of the unemployment insurance measure. He told us what was going to happen and what was going to replace the curtailment of the benefit eligibility period; but he took fine care that he gave us no details. He had no program, and there is nothing I can tell the young people of Atlantic Canada, especially as to what will replace this change.
It is easy to talk about jobs and new creations. Are we going to have LIP ad lib? In some way, are we going to pick up the young people's program? What are we going to do? Some day this session will adjourn. Summer is coming. We might end this portion of it. I would like to know from the Minister of Manpower and Immigration what to tell the people down there and what is coming in place of this. I invite the minister or some of his cabinet colleagues to tell us, before this debate is over, so that we can tell our people what is coming from this disastrous budget.

speakeroldname: Mr. Bob Kaplan (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is a rumour around that the Liberal caucus opposes the tightening-up of unemployment insurance which is taking place in the current budget. I have no intention of representing the views of the Liberal caucus, but in view of the rumour I want to speak for myself and indicate that as a Liberal I very much welcome this part of the budget. In fact, I think we would have had a better unemployment insurance program if even more changes had taken place, and I want to suggest some to the government.
Anyone who criticizes the extent of payments which the government makes to the unemployed needs to be attacked for being a yahoo. After all, what can be wrong with giving payments to people who are out of work? When the program was first proposed I remember the tremendous pressure from the business community which expressed concern about the potential cost of the program and its possible effect on the work ethic. There was an answer. It was said that this kind of criticism was being made by people who were against unemployment insurance. Some people said, "What does the business community know about the work ethic?" Besides, the plan was to be an insurance type plan supported not by taxes but by employer-employee contributions.
During the 1972 election campaign I remember my opponent arguing that in its first year of operation the unemployment insurance program had exceeded its estimated cost of operation by $1 billion. I went through the entire
[Mr. Macquarrie.J
election campaign without contradicting him. He was wrong. The excess was slightly over $600 million. I remember asking myself, after I was defeated, if the government would have introduced the program in the first place if it had known that it would cost in the first year $600 million more than was estimated.
Putting aside the enormous contributions made to the fund by employers and employees, the federal government's contribution to the unemployment insurance fund, or our tax contribution, rose in 1971 from $103 million to an estimated amount for the fiscal year ending in 1976 of $890 million. I understand that the estimated contribution for 1976-77 is $1.7 billion. And that does not include the contribution made by the employer and employee.

speechtext:
Unemployment insurance can be looked on as a great liberal advance. I agree with it. I think unemployment insurance is a program which Canadians are willing to accept; it represents a recognition of liberalism in society. It represents the recognition that while opportunities should be provided for the individual to make the most of himself, to fulfil his life, the grave risks of losing one's livelihood should be shared.
The unemployment insurance program has always been difficult to administer because of its many facets. We consider the job search, and the quality of that search. During the initial period the government encountered understandable difficulties in controlling and administering the new program. Yet with the benefit of hindsight I find it hard to be critical of the way the program was administered. So far as I can see, and I followed the program closely, there are now few difficulties connected with abuse of unemployment insurance. I think the program is well administered and adequately controlled. As I see it, the budget we are considering is not concerned about abuses so much as about initial design problems, if I may put it that way.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I notice a strange ambivalence on the part of hon. members opposite with regard to unemployment insurance.
June 3, 1976

This plan has always enjoyed, in large measure, the support of members on all sides of the House. It puts into practice the principle that we are our brother's keeper. It gives members of our society while unemployed, and seeking an opportunity to return to the work force, the support they deserve.
As I said in the beginning the business community voiced its concern. Now as of 1976 the difficulties connected with the program are widely recognized far beyond the business community and the present budget is designed to correct those very difficulties which are of concern to members of the community at large. No matter which neighbourhood of my constituency I visit, I hear people grumbling about individuals who are on unemployment insurance and who, in the opinion of neighbours, ought to be working or would be working if a genuine incentive existed to find a job. I occasionally hear parents say this sort of thing about young people.
Let me tell the House something that happened to me not long ago. Last Friday afternoon I received six students from my riding. They attend York University. One of them came up here to work in a government department; the job, starting this summer, is to be permanent. The other five were on unemployment insurance. Well, they had been students for the year and, as it turned out, had all worked last summer. Therefore having worked for eight, nine or 12 weeks last summer, they were qualified for and entitled to unemployment insurance if they could not find a job.
I told them that I had seen help wanted ads in shop windows in the shopping centre where my constituency office is located. There were signs saying, "Cashier Wanted," and "Help Wanted," and so on. I asked these young people if they knew about such opportunities, and had tried to take advantage of them. They said to me, "Well, no. This is how we looked for our jobs-we sent out nearly 100 letters to all sorts of businesses, asking for jobs." They said that none of these letters produced an offer of employment; they felt that, having spent nearly $10 on postage in conducting their job search, they were entitled to claim unemployment insurance. I can imagine how parents who work all their lives feel when confronted with a situation like that. But they tried for a job, continued to write letters, and to claim unemployment insurance.
Let me refer to some statistics which the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras) brought to the fore when he spoke the other day. He said that in a majority of cases those who claimed unemployment insurance for the maximum period after eight to 11 weeks of work were able, when their qualifying period ran out, to find employment. A large percentage found work within six weeks. I think that many of them are like the students who came to my office from my part of the city of Toronto. They may not be aware of where to find work. Or, if they were given a greater incentive to find work, many would be able to do so, I am sure.
I think the changes in the plan will benefit regions like mine. The changes proposed by the government are changes in the right direction. They will increase employment, not increase the number of people on welfare. Not only will they lead to increased employment; they will lead to increased productivity in our economy. There are labour shortages in every sector.
The Budget-Mr. Kaplan
I turn now to the problems we encounter in some depressed regions of the country. There the situation is quite different. I understand that there you cannot go into a shopping centre, as you can in Toronto, and find jobs advertised in store windows. It is hard to find work in those areas. The question we must ask ourselves-and the hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. Macquarrie) asked it but without looking at the answers-is this: is unemployment insurance the kind of constructive program which will produce employment in depressed areas of this country, or must we do something else? Instead of institutionalizing employment can we increase productivity in Canada? Shall we continue features which create a sense of entitlement to a pension? In other words, if we do not change the unemployment insurance program will we make Canadians, especially those in the depressed areas, into a nation of pensioners?
By themselves I think unemployment insurance payments are a false solution, a false source of prosperity and stability for the depressed regions of the country. There is a better way. If the hon. member for Hillsborough had listened to the minister, or read his speech, he would know that the government is making solid proposals for job creation, proposals which will bring development to our depressed regions, and programs which ought to be in place in depressed areas in order to create employment. I believe that most Canadians want to work. It is particularly frustrating for the unemployed in the depressed regions of this country because the jobs are not there.
You cannot have a program that is escalating in cost the way this program is and try at the same time to add something new and substantial to the job creation element. When government expenditures just cannot be permitted to grow at their recent historic rate, you have to cut back some programs in order to expand others. In my view nothing can be more rational than to cut back a program like unemployment insurance where the thrust of it is directed toward providing a kind of false alternative to employment, and to try to develop programs that create employment. I very much welcome that. I think you can be a Liberal and welcome that alternative. I very much approve of what the government has done.
Recently I wrote to the minister. I made a number of proposals for amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act which are not anti-liberal, anti-the unemployed, anti-the depressed regions. They are designed to give the government the resources to really do something about the depressed regions and to create a base of employment in those regions.
I recommended lengthening the qualification period. This has been done. It has been lengthened to 12 weeks. When the minister appears before the committee it will be interesting to know how much resources would have been freed if that 12 weeks had been 16 or 20 weeks, as are the qualification periods in use in the other liberal societies of western Europe and the industrialized world.
Second, I suggested adjusting the benefit period, which has been done, so that a shorter benefit period will apply for a shorter labour force attachment period.

June 3, 1976
The Budget-Mr. Kaplan
Third, I suggested that family income should be taken into consideration. This was not done in the budget. I hope it will still be considered. The individual who has no dependants, who is alone, would receive a smaller unemployment payment than the individual who is the sole earner and has a family to look after. For the individual who is a second earner in a family and whose income is not as essential, the payment could be lower.
One would like to see larger payments go to all individuals who are unemployed and who are genuinely searching for work, but we are talking about limited resources. If resources are limited, is it not better to give them to those who need them more, and use the savings to try to create employment, instead of just creating a government pension base for a local economy?
Fourth, I suggested that the government take a look at the situation of part-time and seasonal workers. I do not think the theory of the unemployment insurance system was that a part-time worker and a seasonal worker were to participate in benefits on the same basis as a person who found a full-time job, intended to be a full-time worker, lost that job and is looking for another full-time job. Special rules should apply for people in the work force on a special, temporary, part-time or seasonal basis.
Fifth, I drew the attention of the minister to a special type of unemployment, the layoff. A fair percentage of people who are unemployed and on unemployment insurance do not consider themselves to be unemployed. They consider themselves to be waiting for a recall from the employer who laid then off. Their situation is special. The employer who lays off a person because there is not enough work in the plant, or whatever it is, for the time being, has a responsibility to those employees he hopes to get back when business improves. His responsibility is greater than that of the employer who has had to lay off or fire people or close his business without the intention of recalling them. In a case like that, the laid-off employee should not be treated in the same way as the ordinary hardship case that led us to opt for a very generous unemployment insurance program in the first place.
Finally, I stated to the minister that there was a change which many were advocating that I do not support and do not want to see take place. Say a person earning $10,000, $11,000 or $14,000 a year loses his job. It is suggested that while such persons are looking for a similar job they ought to be forced by the administration to take any job that comes along.
As an example, a person may have worked as a manager in a business that has gone bankrupt. He wants to find another job as a manager. The case is put forward that this person ought to be prepared to take any job rather than go on unemployment insurance. I reject that argument. The unemployment insurance program ought to permit an individual who had a job that required high qualifications to have the opportunity to find a similar kind of job.
If a manager who has been laid off must accept a job as a waiter or something similar, it would be very difficult for him to make a proper job search for the kind of job he is capable of doing and which is more productive in terms of what it does for the economy as well as being more remunerative for him. That individual should not be forced to take any job just to get off unemployment insurance. He

should be given a fair chance to find the kind of job he had before. I was very glad the minister did not go that far in making changes.
I look forward to seeing the bill introduced by the Minister of Manpower and Immigration implementing these two extremely progressive changes. They will free funds which ought to be clearly committed to areas of need and to create employment in areas where we have been providing as an alternative an unemployment insurance base. That is really a dead end or false alternative.
I congratulate the minister, and indicate to him that I very much support what he has done. I consider it to be the kind of liberal approach to improving this plan that has been needed for some time.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is a very dull, ho-hum type of budget. It has done very little, if anything, to excite the Canadian people or to help the economy of the country.
The government is relying on the anti-inflation regulations brought in last October in the hope that they will do something to control inflation in Canada. Even though it campaigned vigorously against any form of controls, last October it saw fit to bring in controls. However, that has not done very much to control inflation in Canada. It has not done anything to get people moving in the proper direction to control inflation in Canada.
The government brought in the budget because it was embarrassed about the length of time that had elapsed since the previous budget. Therefore it felt it should bring one in. It certainly was not very much of a budget.
We see that the main thrust of the budget is directed toward unemployment insurance. We don't really need budgets to debate unemployment insurance. It would have been easy for the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras) to have brought in the necessary proposals to present to parliament in an effort to do something about unemployment insurance. But because the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) could find very little to put in the budget, or because he did not want to find very much, he concentrated on the unemployment insurance aspect. Thus we find ourselves today debating unemployment insurance and the absence of proper administration instead of the economic situation. What we are really discussing is the attempt to fix up the unemployment insurance arrangements which were brought in some years ago by the government, and which are not working.
From time to time the opposition has drawn attention in no uncertain terms to the fact that the unemployment insurance scheme is not working properly. We know the government is concerned about the high cost of the scheme and we realize, too, that there are many people in Canada who are concerned about this aspect. These include, in particular, men and women who keep paying into the fund-for them it is a form of taxation-but who never benefit from unemployment insurance and in fact never use it. They are asking whether it is truly an unemployment insurance program or whether it is really a welfare program in disguise.
June 3, 1976

We also have before us the latest report of the Economic Council of Canada concerning people and jobs. The main thrust of this report is getting people back to work. There is a lot to be said about the psychological aspect when it comes to getting people to work. The minister in his speech yesterday referred to "frictional and structural causes" as part of the reason for the large number of people in receipt of unemployment insurance benefits. Seasonal unemployment, he said, accounted for only a very small percentage of the total and other factors accounted for a much higher percentage. As far as I can determine, "frictional" implies a clash of will, temperament or opinion. This is one of the aspects dealt with in the report of the Economic Council.
What we are really talking about here is the work ethic. There is a clash of wills and opinions. I do not believe the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has done anything to help in the last few years by telling the people of Canada, "You really should be doing your own thing." In many instances, and I think this is notable about a lot of young people in Canada, doing their own thing does not mean working.
I like to look at what is happening in British Columbia today. I think one of the bright spots in the new provincial government there is the minister of labour who has come on very strong and told the people on welfare they should pick up a shovel. It did not go over too well to start with, but the result has been that the attitudes of people working today are considerably different. He designated areas where you could not get welfare. In other words, he told the people they had to go to areas where there was work. Whether it was there or not, they had to be there if they wanted to get welfare. It has made a considerable difference in my riding, especially in a lot of those places where we were having trouble with young people getting together in communes. I talked to the people last week about what is happening in those areas now and they said the communes have disappeared, they are just not there. I talked to business people, to processors and people in packing plants, and they say there is an entirely different feeling today on the part of young people about getting to work because they know they have to work, and they are working. The type of thing the Prime Minister has been saying about doing your own thing has done really nothing to foster the work ethic in Canada. May I call it six o'clock?
At six o'clock the House took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The House resumed at 8 p.m.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at six o'clock I was talking about unemployment insurance and the fact that the government has seen clear to announce amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act in the budget. I was saying that the Economic Council of Canada report concerning people and jobs had reported that a lot of people were on unemployment insurance for frictional and structural reasons. After what the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the government have said, that you do your own thing in Canada and you really don't have to work, it is understandable that the Economic Council should find that there are frictional reasons for people being on unemploy-
The Budget-Mr. Whittaker
ment insurance. "Frictional" really means, as far as I can determine, a clash of will, temperaments and opinions. I think if this government wants to convince people that they should work, it should not be speaking in this manner but rather should be telling them that it is a good thing to work, that there are many businesses in Canada that need workers. There are many workers who are willing to go to work but are not working under the shadow of the type of ethic that the Prime Minister advocates, that of do your own thing.
On November 5 we were debating unemployment insurance and I was lucky enough to speak that day. I was talking about the large amount of money that is being spent on unemployment insurance today, almost $4 billion, and about some of the reasons why there was such high unemployment. The member for New Westminster (Mr. Leggatt) in speaking after me twisted, I think, quite a lot of what I said, and argued that I had said that the reason there was a high unemployment insurance cost in Canada was because of abuses. He said "I defy the hon. member to cost the abuses and to tell me what percentage of the deficit is a direct result thereof".
I was very pleased to read in the review of the Economic Council "People and Jobs" that 0.7 per cent of the unemployed are on unemployment insurance today because of the laxity of the program. There are 70,000 people estimated to be on unemployment insurance because of this, and if you cost it into the total cost of the unemployment insurance it would amount to some $350 million. I think that should be proof enough for the hon. member for New Westminster, if he wants to take the time to read that portion and understand really what were talking about at that time.
I do not think that what the government is trying to do in its budget is going to do very much about that portion of the people and the laxity of the program. I think much more will have to be done if it is going to service that area. It has attacked the length of time, requiring a longer length of time for people to qualify for unemployment insurance. I am not sure that is the correct way. The government says it will save $330 million in this manner. If a person is legitimately off work he is suffering, and this is not the area where the attack should take place.
I am certainly pleased to hear that the government is now getting around to wanting to put Manpower and unemployment insurance together again. This is a real necessity, and the emphasis must be placed on Manpower, getting these 70,000 people back in the work force and gainfully employed. Some people may ask where they are going to work. There are lots of jobs if you have people with the right attitude. Much of the work being done in Canada today is not being done on time, is taking longer than it should. This is because people in business will not stand for harassment, and will not allow those people with the wrong attitude to work for them. I think there is quite an area in this regard for people who want to work.
We also know that many mines, not just in the remote areas, but in areas such as my riding, do not have enough people working because people will not go there. Of course they will not go when somebody else tells them they

June 3, 1976
The Budget-Mr. Whittaker
should be doing their own thing, and when there is a tremendous unemployment insurance and welfare scheme on which they can fall back. All these jobs must be filled, and I think with the right attitude it would not be too hard to fill them.
The minister announced that he is going to have another $100 million for LIP this year. This is good, providing it is spent properly. I hope he has read the review of the Economic Council of Canada, "People and Jobs", in which it is said that the government should enlist provincial governments, local governments, municipalities, and business organizations in order to carry out these programs. Rather than having a program under which the government asks the people what they want, it should co-operate with these various levels of government and business because they know what is needed in the various areas. I entirely agree with this suggestion, and this is what we must do if we are to spend the money and get the job done properly.
We should also spend this money on programs that last a year and longer, rather than just on projects or programs that last a few months, with people going back on unemployment insurance at their conclusion. People in these local areas are aware of the local needs and they will accept the responsibility of seeing that the job is done well.
Nothing at all was said in the budget about agriculture. Probably most hon. members will not remember what was said in the throne speech, because that was delivered in November, 1974, going on two years ago. At one time we had two sessions a year; now we have two years a session. I suggest this is not good because the government tends to forget what it proposed at the beginning.
In that throne speech of November, 1974, the government stressed that there should be incentives for farmers, with stabilization of income and markets. We all know of the demonstration which took place here today. The government should go back and read what it said in 1974. Had it meant what it said then we would not be experiencing the type of demonstration we saw today.
Every farm commodity grown in Canada that I know of has a more distressed price today than in November, 1974, perhaps with the exception of grains, and I am given to understand they are becoming more distressed.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That's not true.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Somebody suggests that is not true. I wish he would get up and tell me of an area where it is not true. I would be very glad to hear about it, but I do not think the hon. member can tell me.
The cattle producer is in an even more distressed position than the producers of fruits and vegetables. The fruit and vegetable canning industry is certainly in a distressed position today, particularly in British Columbia. I suggest the reason is that cheap imports are coming into Canada as a result of the cheap food policy of the government. Obviously the government did not mean what it said in the throne speech of November, 1974. It is carrying on with the same type of cheap food policy it had years ago.
If there is someone else in the world who can produce cheaper than in Canada the government suggests we should bring in their products virtually free of any encum-

brance. The farmers in my area used to say, and I think this is also accurate today, that Canada is a saint in a world of sinners when it comes to the import-export trade. We put no encumbrances, or very few, on imported farm produce. Other countries in the world put total embargoes on our products when they see fit. They always seem able to find some kind of gimmick or means of putting an embargo on Canadian produce. Canada does not do this.
In this budget we find that the government intends to remove the tariff or reduce it in respect of pork. Every time a farm commodity reaches a position where our farmers are able to make a little bit of money the government reduces the tariff, allowing imports to come in, knocking the heck out of our farmers. The government has done this before and is doing it again. Pork is a product on which the producers are able to make a few dollars today. Now the government is taking the tariff off.
Let us just take the example of canned products being imported. There is a flood of cheap canned products coming into western Canada today. As a result the producers there still have last year's stocks on hand. The farmers want to produce, and the government suggests that production should be up in Canada. But the farmers cannot produce because there are no cans to be filled, and those that were filled last year are still sitting on the shelves. This is a result of the importation of cheap canned products. The farmers are wondering why they are not getting contracts from the producers. They are not getting them because the warehouses are filled with last year's products.
