subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
This letter is from Mrs. D. L. Milne Cannery Limited. It states:
As the government has stock piles of various foods for Acts of God (i.e. powdered milk), could the idea be engendered to use pears, packed in No. 10 cans, 100 oz. of fruit and liquid sugar.
The 1976 pear crop is going to be large and the canners pack will be small due to foreign dumping. I am suggesting that each canner be allotted a quota of this surplus product and the government show originality in having such a useful and nutritional product with long keeping quality, available for distribution (the rats cannot eat this).
This year the pear producers will be very hard pressed because they still have on hand their stocks of the canning crop from last year.
We hear about the tariff being removed from pork. This is taking place at a time when pork producers are making a little more money. We also note that the tariff is being removed from bananas. Bananas are in direct competition with the fruits and vegetables grown in Canada. Bananas are grown in a country where there is cheap labour. They flood the Canadian market, and now we note that those who ship them into Canada are to have an advantage. Many manufacturers in Canada are in exactly the same position. As soon as they establish a good business in which they can show a profit the government reduces the tariff, and consequently imports into Canada do much to inhibit their business. Therefore these manufacturers lose the incentive to increase their business. There are many such examples in Canada of businesses which are having difficulty in competing with imports. The government is doing absolutely nothing to help these businesses.
Then there is the matter of transportation. Transportation costs are much higher here than in the United States, and we have difficulty competing in this area. I do not see anything in the budget to relieve this situation. I do not see the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) doing anything about this. It is very difficult for farmers and manufacturers in Canada to compete with the competition from outside Canada.
Although we have been told there is to be a cut in government spending we find that government spending is higher. Many people believe that a large part of the inflation in Canada is caused by government spending. In the Globe and Mail of March 11, 1976, there is a story about how the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Chretien) got the ministers of various departments to cut their budgets. He said he did it by gimmicks and tactics. He added that if the ministers did not subscribe to what he was asking, he would take the matter to cabinet. I think that is a good story. However, when we look at the situation we find that budgets have not been cut. We find that we are spending more in Canada. I think the minister should have gone to cabinet if he wants to cut the budgets of the various departments, because people are saying that the spending
The Budget-Hon. J. C. Munro
of the government is the cause of much of the inflation in Canada today.
The Employers' Council of British Columbia in its review of the budget said it is too bad that the government has not developed a more realistic level for the Canadian dollar, and new job creation through the encouragement of investment. The Canadian dollar is high in relation to what it really should be, especially if the government would cut back on its spending. A high Canadian dollar favours imports into Canada rather than exports from Canada. This is really an exporting nation. The government should be doing everything it can to make sure that we are able to export.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Order, please. I regret to interrupt the hon. member but his allotted time has expired. He may continue with the unanimous consent of the House. Does the hon. member have unanimous consent?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Agreed.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Thank you very much. I shall try to be as brief as I can. Our trade deficit is very high. We should be taking action to ensure that the Canadian dollar favours exports rather than imports into Canada. In the budget our deficit is reported to be $3.3 billion, but really when all the needs of the governments and its borrowings are tallied up one can see that it is really $4.5 billion. Because of this interest rates are high, and the dollar is at a high level. This dampens the export trade.
We hear much talk about energy. A high tax has been placed on large cars and air conditioners. This is very good. A manufacturer in my area who manufactures wood-burning stoves made a submission to the Minister of Finance that the excise tax be removed from wood-burning stoves. There is no excise tax on oil burners or gas burners of any kind, but there is a tax on wood-burning stoves. Wood in Canada is a renewable resource. I would have thought this tax would have been removed, especially since the minister wrote me a letter in which he said:
In the event that the sales tax relief you seek can only be provided through an amendment to the Excise Tax Act regulations, please be assured that your representation will be reviewed when amendments to these regulations are next under consideration.
I was very disappointed that there was nothing to this effect in the budget. Mr. Speaker, I could go on and on but I am very grateful that I was granted extended time.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The hon. Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro).

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: We have the heavies tonight.

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Munro (Minister of Labour):
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That, coming from another one, Mr. Speaker!
I am glad to have the opportunity to bring out a few facts in this debate in support of the budget presented by my colleague, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald). I think there are a few aspects of this budget, when seen in context of our wage and price control program and other elements of economic policy which show that these policies

June 3, 1976
The Budget-Hon. J. C. Munro
have worked very much to the benefit of organized and unorganized workers.
I think it is well to keep in mind that some people have alleged that the organized and unorganized worker has not been receiving-certainly in the last months-an adequate share of the gross national product. Statistics show that this is a fallacy; in fact labour's share under this government has not only been maintained in terms of its percentage share of the Gross National Product but also in terms of national income. Since the inception of the controls it has actually gone up in current dollars without the inflationary factor taken out, and incomes have gone up in real terms once the inflationary factor has been taken out. If this is true, then some of the statements that are being made throughout the country to the effect that it is the policy of the government, or it is the end result of a wage and price control system and of this budget, to cut down the organized workers' percentage share of the gross national product in relation to incomes, are fallacious.
All hon. members should be aware of the statistics that back up this argument. I do not believe it is in the interests of any hon. member, irrespective of his or her political persuasion, to perpetrate what are erroneous impressions and, although perhaps not intentionally, to deceive the Canadian public about the situation. Before I go into some of these statistics, Mr. Speaker, I think it would be wise to take into account some of the background factors that I am sure were in the mind of the Minister of Finance, and indeed in all our minds when we brought in this budget.
We recognized one central thing, that the crucial national need was to gear down the rate of inflation without impeding economic recovery. This was the way to ensure job security and, in the long run, to combat unemployment. In an uncontrolled inflationary situation there can be no assurance of job security or that any policies will work to cut down an unacceptably high rate of unemployment.
Let me enumerate some of these factors, Mr. Speaker. First, there is no doubt that what we faced as a government, and what all of us faced as parliamentarians, was the unease last October when this program was introduced. The trade union movement and the union leadership felt their position was untenable. The leadership was vulnerable because it had led the membership into long term agreements-some for two or three years. The membership were coming out of those agreements to find that they had fallen behind the rate of inflation. They had endeavoured to anticipate it when they entered into agreements but it turned out to be higher than anticipated, and so the leadership was exposed for having led membership into agreements through which they had fallen behind.
I think it would be a natural thing for the union leadership-and if I were a union leader I would have done the same thing-to predict for 1976 and 1977 the very worst rate of inflation, and then endeavour to build in protection against it in the collective agreements. Of course that can be a self-fulfilling prophecy. If you have to predict the worst and protect against it, inevitably the worst will occur.
The stability of the union leadership, to say nothing about the real earnings of the workers, was very fragile, and this had to be corrected. Our economic policies, includ-

ing the budget and restraint program, were designed to restore the needed stability to workers and their leaders.
The second factor is also apparent,and I think the budget takes it into account as does the wage and price controls program, and that is the plight of the unorganized worker. Organized workers have their spokesmen, and some very effective ones at that, but unorganized workers are often on fixed incomes, or on incomes that do not keep up with the rate of inflation because they do not have spokesmen. They were some of the prime victims of a destructive inflationary process.
I think the third factor in the back of our minds when we not only brought in the restraint program but brought in a neutral budget in terms of the economic stabilizer, was that we recognized that the budget is just one element-it is complementary to the wage and price control scheme and reflects on the other elements that go into an antiinflationary program. I do not have to repeat what the other elements are; the Minister of Finance has dealt with them. They include fiscal and monetary policies, governmental expenditure policies, and structural policies.
The fourth factor that formed part of the background when we decided upon our economic policies was the fact that we must protect the real earnings of the workers, both organized and unorganized. That is what I referred to in a preliminary way in my opening remarks. I think it would be well to note that when we brought in the restraint program, labour's share of the gross national product was at its peak. There has been some suggestion that this scheme was anti-labour in the sense that it was designed to cut down labour's share, or that it was brought in at the low point in the cycle and thus they were cut down while other elements were allowed to expand. That led to some of the mythology that this program was primarily visited upon the backs of the workers.
The facts from Statistics Canada with respect to the workers' share of the Gross National Product-this is a distribution of national income in the context of percentage of Gross National Product-show that in 1975 when we brought in the control program the workers' share in terms of incomes was 56 per cent of the Gross National Product. In 1974 it was 53.9 per cent. In 1973 it was 53.9 per cent. In 1972 it was 55.1 per cent-still lower than the 56 per cent in 1975 when we brought in the program. In 1970 it was 54.5 per cent. If you trace labour's share of the Gross National Product from 1962 to 1975 you will see that we brought in the program when labour's share was at its peak in terms of a percentage of the Gross National Product. This means that the program was not brought in at a low point, in terms of the statistics, of labour's share, but at the high point, and if that share is going up it stands to reason that somebody else is de-escalating.
Indeed, if one wants to look at the profit statistics during that year, 1975, when we brought in the program, profits were 11.5 per cent of the Gross National Product. In 1974 they were 13 per cent. What this points out is that the program was brought in when labour was receiving a high share and profits were declining.
If we start from there, I think it is useful to note just what happened since that time under the controls program.
June 3, 1976

I think it can be pointed out that instead of workers being cut back in terms of real earnings after taking the inflationary factor out, their share has been going up quite substantially. In other words, the inflationary process has no longer been eroding their purchasing power. Under the restraint program they are getting tangible gains in terms of real disposable income. However, before getting into that, I would like to indicate again the fact that labour was at its highest plateau when we brought in this program.
If one wants to look at a history of what has happened when we talk about labour's share of national income from 1975 to 1976, we brought this program in when labour's share of the national income was 73 per cent. In 1974 it was 71.6 per cent. In 1973 it was 71.7 per cent, so in the last three years it was at some of its highest levels. I might just point out that in 1960 it was hovering around 69 per cent. In 1964 it was 69 per cent. Back in 1946 it was 62 per cent. We brought in this program in 1975 when labour's share was 73 per cent.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That's too high.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That gives some indication of the fallacy of what some people would lead us to believe.
I think some other statistics are interesting. Again I am referring to measures of real earnings on a quarterly basis to indicate just how well the workers have done in terms of the effectiveness of some of the economic policies of the government. Let us look at 1975. In the first quarter workers' real earnings had gone up 2.5 per cent. In the second quarter they went up 3.8 per cent. In the third quarter they went up 2.5 per cent, and then in the quarter in which the program began in terms of real earnings the workers' share had gone up 3.2 per cent. This is average real earnings with the inflationary factor taken out.
I think I mentioned the first quarter of 1976. That is the quarter after the anti-inflationary program came into effect, and the workers' real earnings were up 3.6 per cent. Recent statistics I looked at as late as this afternoon indicated that in the month of March over the previous month, which was 3.6 per cent, the rise was 4.1 per cent in real terms after the inflation factor was taken out. Surely this spells out something, and if we take this in the context of the settlements which are now being arrived at since the program came in, the workers have never been in a better position, from an economic point of view, that they are at present under the economic policies of the government.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The average settlements being approved by the Anti-Inflation Board are in the area of approximately 1 per cent against the arithmetic guidelines, and this is because of the historical relationship factors and the special consideration factors which were taken into account, certainly during the early months of the program, and still are. So let us say we are running roughly around 13 per cent, with a majority of the collective agreements being entered into by the parties falling below that. However, in percentage terms, let us say 13 per cent. Yet the inflationary rate this last April as compared with the previous April is now down to 8.9 per cent.
The Budget-Hon. J. C. Munro
If the inflationary rate is down to 8.9 per cent, and the workers and salary and wage earners of this country are currently receiving roughly 13 per cent, is it any wonder that in terms of real disposable income after the inflation factor is taken out they now have a purchasing power 4.1 per cent higher than they had before? That is one of the most marked increases at any time since 1971 on a quarterly basis.
When some of my friends-and they are my friends-in the labour movement argue that the budget, in terms of it being a stabilizer with its primary aim to cut down the inflationary process, and that the controls program are somehow designed to limit labour's share or cut it back, statistics at the time we brought in the program and the statistics currently coming out would indicate exactly the contrary.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: They don't believe that.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I believe that this is the real basis. I have the statistics. My hon. friend says they do not believe this. These are statistics the CLC uses, and I am using them to inform my colleagues in the House. Labour has its economists, too. If they wish to argue with them, I would welcome that. I would welcome a detailed examination of this on their part because I think they would then have the intellectual honesty to perpetuate no longer what is fundamentally a falsehood in terms of what this program is doing for real incomes for the organized and unorganized workers of this country.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I think that this is the basis upon which some of us on this side of the House would claim that a majority of the workers of this country are prepared to go along with this program. They saw what happened to the purchasing power of their dollar under the inflationary process prior to the introduction of wage and price controls, and they saw what would happen in the inflationary process if our budgetary measures-not as introduced by my colleague, the Minister of Finance- fueled the flame of inflation. That would cut down drastically their purchasing power in real terms, which for many of them had been their very unhappy experience in the first few years of the 1970's. Now the workers are receiving one of the most marked increases in real earnings since the program was brought in.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I think this is one of the bases upon which we can legitimately count for a majority of workers getting behind this program, or at least going along with it. This is not to suggest for one minute that if the organized labour leadership in this country, which is highly regarded, for some reasons wishes to ignore the statistics and tries to arouse its members into some type of general strike for a day as a political weapon, the organized workers are going to humiliate their leaders by leaving them exposed and not backing them to a certain degree. I think there is a sufficient feeling of solidarity in the labour movement so that perhaps for a day this could happen, or partially happen. I do not think even they would expect 100 per cent adherence. The labour move-

June 3, 1976
The Budget-Mr. Horner
ment of this country is not more monolithic than any other organization; and in view of statistics showing real gains for the workers of this country I believe they will have some difficulty.
I also believe that it would not be in the interests of the labour movement, its leadership, membership, or in the interest of the country to embark on that process of confrontation which would alienate various elements of the Canadian community from the labour movement, that movement which has contributed so much to the economic well-being of this country.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes, but you are only controlling labour's wages. Who else is being controlled?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You can make your speech later on.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
In conclusion, if the Canadian labour movement meet with us around the middle of June, and I have indicated they are willing to do this, we can assure them that it is not the government's policy to decrease or cut back on labour's share either of the Gross National Product or national income. If they can be so convinced on the basis of the statistics I have put before the House, and we can show them that under this program, in real terms, workers' wages and salaries have gone up, perhaps they can be convinced that it is indeed the government's policy to protect in real terms the wages of all workers in this country.
If we could so lay a solid basis for co-operation we could set up the sort of mechanisms to which my colleague, the Minister of Finance, referred in the budget-structural mechanisms for consultation. This idea was the highlight of the Quebec manifesto of the CLC. It suggested how labour could participate with the government in the economic and social policy formation which will evolve during the post-control period. It seems to me that that was a most significant position for the Canadian labour movement to adopt. Mr. Speaker, they want to be involved; they want to be consulted; they want assurance that the government will respond, and that there will be an ongoing basis for such consultation. This may mean that in future we shall see less of the element of confrontation, less of the adversary approach in relations between labour and the government of the day.
Considering this program's record of protecting the organized and unorganized workers, I think it can lay the solid base for ensuring that in future labour's share of our income in real terms does not decrease but continues to increase, and that labour will get its share of the rewards of productivity as this country prospers.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when I listened to the budget speech I tried to ascertain the real purpose of the budget. Did the minister try to plot a course for this country to follow? Was he trying to plot a course for the Liberal party? What was the purpose of the budget? As I sat here, listening to the minister make his speech on budget night, I could not help thinking that he was talking to himself. He read a long speech very quickly, mainly to himself. The minister was a changed man, not the man we used to know. When he was Minister of Energy, Mines and
(Mr. Munro (Hamilton East).]
Resources, he stuck out his chin, gave the facts, and told Canadians what he thought was good for them and the country. On budget night he was a changed man, talking only to himself, as if conscious that in his first budget address he had little to say to the country, and still less to give it. All this was clear to me on budget night, and is evident if one studies the budget.
A budget has a purpose, Mr. Speaker. It should provide direction to those things the government thinks important. And what does the government think is important? To what does it wish to direct the people's attention?
As I look at the world and consider Canada's role in the world, two things strike me. First, the world is greatly concerned about energy supplies and energy costs. As well, the world is greatly concerned about food supplies. We must ask are we capable of providing food for the underdeveloped people of the world? In addition Canada and the United States are greatly concerned about balance of payments difficulties. The budget address dealt not at all with the question of food supplies, dealt not at all with our agricultural industry and our capability of providing food for ourselves and other peoples of the world not as fortunate as we are, and dealt inadequately with the question of energy. We were told about the 100 per cent write-off provision designed to encourage companies to explore for minerals, oil, and gas. Really, that is a small measure for dealing with the over-all energy picture.
Most Canadians ask themselves this question: will lack of reasonably priced energy supplies limit our growth potential in the years ahead? The minister did not deal with that. He spoke of the high cost of energy, but did not go beyond that. He did not put forward solutions to our problem. He may have hinted at the existence of the problem but did not say how it should be solved. Most Canadians who are prepared to look down the road wonder if the high cost of energy will in future prevent our enjoying our present high standard of living. The minister did not deal with that question, and did not answer it. As I say, he hinted at the existence of the problem, suggested we are concerned about the rate at which we consume energy, suggested somewhat simplified solutions, but did not deal in detail with the problem.
He suggested that our productivity is slightly lower than that of the United States, that we were capable of catching up, that the American economy was doing very well and would bail us out. To met it was a shallow budget. Many newspapers have described it as a dead, a dull budget. The May 29 edition of the Financial Post said that this is an inadequate budget:
... especially since the federal government is expecting a huge 26 per cent increase in its personal income tax take during the current fiscal year? After all, there is nothing in the budget which would give unemployment a whisker of a chance of coming down.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What is the hon. member quoting?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I quoted an article in the Financial Post, to enlighten hon. members opposite and the hon. member who just interrupted, and to substantiate what I said about the budget. I feel that it will do absolutely nothing to decrease unemployment in Canada, already running at the rate of 7.4 per cent.
June 3, 1976

In his column, which appears in many papers, Douglas Fisher castigated the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) for his budget. He said that Ottawa awaits with rising hope the American recovery becoming a boom. He further stated that the minister did not attempt to deal with the economic problems in Canada. I agree.
The minister suggested lengthening the qualifying period before a worker can collect unemployment insurance from eight to 12 weeks. The government has the habit of doing one thing, causing a great deal of concern, then patching it up by undoing what it should not have done in the first place. That is certainly true in this instance.
As one writer stated, one will go off Ottawa's pogey and on to the local dole. That may well be the case in many of the high unemployment areas. The minister certainly did not attempt to deal with the fiscal disparity that exists within various regions of Canada.
In the past year the government has added to a high cost economy. One need only look at the legislation dealt with in this House during this lengthy session which has lasted almost two years. Nearly every piece of legislation has contributed to growth in the civil service.
When looking at the figures I was astonished to see that the staff in the Post Office has grown by 15,000 in the past few years. I used to think that part of the problem creating the unrest in that department was the fact that automation would cost a lot of workers their jobs. That certainly has not been the case. Automation must have been completely stopped in the Post Office. It certainly has not contributed to any greater efficiency; many Canadians will attest to that. We do not have a situation where the government has been hiring less people.
The minister suggested the concept of again bringing together unemployment insurance and the employment department. There is an article in the Globe and Mail about this. The government separated these two departments a few years ago. Now that it is bringing them together again, we are expected to hail it as the great saviour. The Unemployment Insurance Commission will be grouped with the employment department. The word "unemployment" will be dropped completely. However, the government is only uniting what it divided.
What happened after the division? There was a tremendous growth in the civil service. In one department there were 10,000 civil servants, and 11,000 in the other. By again bringing them together there will be a duplication of services. According to an article in the Globe and Mail and reprinted in the Calgary Albertan, the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras) said that there will be a duplication of much of the work. Can we expect a reduction in the number of civil servants as a result of grouping these departments? One official says that we can only look for a no-growth situation.
If we analyse the problem of inflation we see that the cause is excessive government spending. At the time of the last budget the government budgeted for a $1.5 billion deficit. It had a $5 billion deficit. It is now budgeting for a $4.5 billion deficit, saying that is less than we had in the last year. However, this is greatly above what it budgeted in its last budget. If its current prediction is as far out, we
The Budget-Mr. Horner
are apt to have a $10 billion deficit. How do I reach that quick conclusion? For one thing there is no mention in the budget of the social changes which the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) talked about with his provincial counterparts this past week. There is no mention of that $375 million expenditure.
There are many omissions with regard to expenditures that the government fully intends to make within the next year. The budget is only a guide for government expenditures. The Minister of Finance deliberately omitted many known expenditures that the government will incur during the next year. The social program under the Minister of National Health and Welfare is just one example that comes to mind. Expenditures in the field of transportation are another. There are many more that will crop up and, therefore, the budgetary deficit suggested will be completely erroneous.
The minister stated that we must attempt to become energy self-sufficient. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie) spoke of that this afternoon. The budget dealt with three matters with regard to energy. It eased the clamp on dividends, allowing dividends to be paid as high as 8 per cent. At the same time it limited profits to 85 per cent of the base period. Therefore there will not be many companies able to pay dividends of more than 8 per cent. The limit on dividends should not have been set in the first place. This is an old habit of government ministers-creating a problem, solving it, and then expecting the Canadian public to hail them as great saviours. All they do is save themselves from their past actions.
The minister stated Canadians can look forward to a period in the future when interest rates will come down. He alluded to this several places in the budget. However, he did not state how or why they could come down other than to say that the American economy was picking up and we can take heart from that.
In the budget address the minister also stated that if you use your spare money to drill your own gas or oil well, or dig your own mine, you can write off 100 per cent of the exploration costs. That is supposed to be a bonus or gift to the oil companies and those provinces that have energy resources. It might also be a boon to those provinces which have potential in the mining industry. The minister mentioned exploration costs, but not development costs. Speaking for the oil and gas industry, that action is about 25 years too late. Had it been done 25 years ago many Canadians would have gotten into the oil industry to a much greater degree.
Another feature in the budget worthy of comment is the clause allowing Petro-Canada to pick up 25 per cent of the land in northern Canada in an attempt to Canadianize the oil industry. Why did the government not make that concession available to all Canadian oil companies, not only to the national oil company but to groups of Canadians willing to form a company and take part in exploration and development? To my mind the big question in the minds of Canadians who are concerned about this subject is: how extensive are the reserves in the north? The minister made reference to the need for more accurate reporting. The government is to demand more accurate information

June 3, 1976
The Budget-Mr. Horner
from the oil companies. The suggestion, I suppose, is that exaggerated claims have been made with respect to reserves or that there are reserves which have been found but not reported.
I listened to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources this afternoon and noted that he failed to deal in any way with the issue of the Mackenzie gas pipeline. Does the government want this pipeline? Two years ago the present Minister of Finance said it did-that it wanted the pipeline but was anxious to go about it in the right way. Now the dilemma is compounded by the necessity of considering a number of alternatives. There is the Polar gas route; the Arctic gas consortium wants to build a pipeline and we find a consortium which proposes to build through the Yukon and then branch into oil lines already existing in Alberta. I see that Foothills Gas is applying for a licence also. But nowhere in the budget did the government attempt to provide any degree of security for these operations, or any certainty as to the manner in which it proposed to go about settling native land claims in the region so that work might proceed and much needed resources might be brought on stream perhaps by the year 1982.
It is all well and good to talk about the energy crisis with which Canada might well be confronted in the years to come, but it is evident that the government is prepared to do very little about it other than attempt to bring greater Canadian content into the oil industry. I wish to deal with that aspect, too.
If we are faced in this country with a severe balance of payments problem and if we, in effect, import money from abroad to maintain our growth rate and the value of our dollar, we are virtually selling off a little bit of Canada each year. That is exactly what happened last year. The balance of payments went against us by some $5 billion. Foreign capital was enticed into Canada by high interest rates and it bought a little more of Canada in the process.
The government has got to set its house in order. It must reduce its expenditures. In his budget speech the minister sought to reassure us that he would try to keep federal expenditure in line with the growth in the Gross National Product. As far as I am concerned his assurances are not good enough. I saw little in the budget to convince me he was deeply concerned about the energy question. He told the House that in order to take the economy in hand he would give the Anti-Inflation Board more power by allowing the use of a different accounting system based on actual profits, something which would make it much easier for the Board to control the economy. To my mind, when I look at the economies of the six major countries in the OECD and compare what is happening there with what is happening in Canada, it becomes evident that we did not need an Anti-Inflation Board in any case.
The problem was caused mainly by the government's inept handling of the economy, and in particular by its too rapid acceleration of the money supply. It attempted to blame the unions and union demands for higher wages, but prior to last October the biggest culprits in the area of wage settlements were the public service unions, not the private sector. The public servants gained from the government larger settlements before October, 1975, than did the private sector. They were ahead by several percentage points. The government across the way created this prob-

lem and then brought in the Anti-inflation Board in an attempt to solve it. We, in turn, are supposed to hail them as some kind of saviour. Well, there is an interesting quotation in the current issue of Business Week dealing with inflation prospects:
After a period of high inflation the inevitable resultTs an abortive effort to impose price controls and an eventual collapse into a managed economy.
I suggest this is what we are getting into now. We are passing through a period of control following the government's careless handling of the economy. We are passing through that stage and moving into a wholly managed economy. How much better off shall we be as Canadians? I suggest we shall all be worse off because the government consistently fails to recognize the basic needs of our society.
It is all very well for the Minister of Energy to say, as he did this afternoon, that he is putting forward an energy strategy, and outlining the use of energy in Canada and in the Western world over the past number of years. In the 70 years before the war the demand for energy in all forms grew at a rate of 3.2 per cent a year. Since the war our energy demand has grown at the rate of about 5 per cent. The minister of energy says we have to get this down to 2 per cent. How does he suggest we do so?
The Minister of Finance in his budget thought we should all get wind chargers and rely on the wind. Well, Mr. Speaker, prairie farmers know all about wind chargers. Many a prairie farmer has climbed them often and found great difficulty in storing energy in the batteries provided. Whether the government sponsors the building of huge wind chargers or not, I question whether any significant saving of energy would be realized; I suppose the minister was putting forward that idea with half a smile on his face. Storage of solar energy presents a similar problem.
The minister did not indicate how many millions of dollars the government was prepared to put into research in the area of wind energy or solar energy. He did say, though, that a tax of $100 would be placed on air conditioners because air conditioners in automobiles used up more gas. He thought the tax would discourage the use of such air conditioners. Mr. Speaker, it will not discourage the use of one air conditioner in one automobile. It is nothing but an added tax on those who feel that they need, or can afford, an air conditioner.
The same applies to the tax on heavier automobiles. It will not discourage to any noticeable extent the use of heavier automobiles, particularly in the part of the country from which I come. Before the minister gets that statement wrong, let me make it abundantly clear that on many of our rural roads in Canada heavier automobiles are sought by many people, since with a higher clearance they stand up to the bumps and rough gravel much better than some of the smaller cars. The minister is really placing a tax on the people who want to drive heavier automobiles. This is a tax that will reap his department an additional $35 million; it is really an added tax. This tax will fall mostly upon the members of the agricultural industry, who use rural roads and I suppose feel they need a heavier car.
June 3, 1976

Getting back to the subject of energy, at no place in his budget is there any encouragement for the use of coal to a greater extent. The minister of energy this afternoon also made no mention of this. Nova Scotia, for example, derives all its electricity from oil-driven generators. I do not blame Nova Scotia for this because at one time oil was a pretty cheap commodity; in fact it was so for about 40 years. Did the minister outline in his budget some of the dangers of this state of affairs continuing? Did he mention how much coal Canada has? Did he allow for a bonus if the maritimes switched to coal-driven generators? No, Mr. Speaker, the budget makes no mention of that.
It is interesting to note how much coal was used in days gone by. Up until 1940 70 per cent of the world's energy was generated by the use of coal. Today the world uses twice as much energy derived from oil and gas. I think in the long term the situation must be reversed; more and more must we make greater use of coal.
How does Canada stack up against the rest of the world in economic matters? I see Your Honour is about ready to rise, so let me conclude my remarks briefly by saying that four of the six major countries that are members of the OECD are doing better than Canada, namely, the United States, Germany, Japan, and France. All of this is being accomplished without any use being made of an anti-inflation board or the kind of rigid controls that the government has imposed upon Canadians as a result of its own carelessness in the last two years.

speakeroldname: Mr. Irenee Pelletier (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, during the budget debate last spring, my remarks dealt almost exclusively with the textile problems in Canada and on looking them over, I find great progress has been made since then.
I had then suggested three methods likely, it seemed to me, to improve the textile situation. Firstly, that the Textile and Clothing Board's recommendations, following an investigation in a textile sector where it is proven beyond any doubt that the Canadian textile industry has been injured, should be accepted as such by the Canadian government. Secondly, that the Textile and Clothing Board become a permanent board. Thirdly, that we decide once and for all the share of the Canadian market for the Canadian textile producers.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I had hoped that if we were to realize those three means of action I had detailed, there could be a tripartite meeting with government, management and labour to examine in depth the issue of the textile and clothing industry in Canada, with a view to developing a common objective and in the shortest possible time a real national textile policy in Canada.
Perhaps it is not necessarily because of this speech that, twelve months later, it was considered important to proceed with that suggestion. Nevertheless more than a month ago the Canadian government decided, to establish a committee to examine the textile situation in Canada and submit recommendations before the end of this month to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce prior to the development of a Canadian textile policy.
The Budget-Mr. Pelletier
I want to congratulate the minister for having taken that initiative and having, somehow answered the wishes expressed repeateadly by the textile workers, that is, specifically, that the government should adopt a truly Canadian policy in that area to spare the textile workers the continuous uncertainties that have existed for so many years.
The problems brought up in last year's discussions are exactly the same this year. And the solutions proposed at that time still seem to be applicable, as far as I can see. Since the textile policy was announced in 1970, we have been under the impression that the recommendations of the then minister were not implemented and that no real progress has been made.
How is it, Mr. Speaker, that every now and then we have to come back to Parliament to remind people that all is not well in that area, that the Textile and Clothing Board has produced still another report, adding to the scores of reports already published and that, in the final analysis, most of these studies and recommendations, whether they are implemented or not, have done little to remedy the situation in this industry?
When I am told that steps are being taken to cope with some of the difficulties, when in fact every year the number of jobs is decreasing and competition is stiff from abroad, and not only from under-developed countries but from the United States, I wonder whether those people who handle textiles in the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce really and truly want to help that industry progress.
I appreciate the announcement made by the minister a few weeks ago, specifically, that a special committee was being set up to look into the situation in the Canadian textile industry. A quick survey of the last six years reveal that good intentions were very ably expressed on several occasions but that, actually, the industry perhaps does not even fare as well as it did a few years ago. We are justified to reserve our judgment on the final brief which should be tabled within thirty days or so. It certainly is the responsibility of the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Jamieson) to determine what kind of textile policy we should have in Canada, and this must be done in cooperation with Canadian manufacturers, textile workers, importers, exporters and the government.
Without the participation of all these people, it is very possible that the new Canadian textile policy will not reflect the real situation of that manufacturing sector. In the last year, in several parts of Canada and particularly of Quebec, many unions have studied the domestic situation very seriously. I have had the opportunity many times to meet textile workers during seminars and study sessions in the constituency I have the honour to represent in this House. Each time, I met workers who are aware of the problem caused very often by imports on the domestic market.
Very recently, the Centrale des syndicats democratiques produced an in-depth study on the textile industry in Canada, which affects more than 200,000 workers, more than half of them being in Quebec. The area of the Eastern Townships is dominated to a very large extent by the

June 3, 1976
The Budget-Mr. Pelletier
textile industry and the economic health of this area still depends on the vitality of the textile industry. Now, it is very easy to have a fairly precise idea of the economy in the Eastern Townships when we see that the textile industry has been affected for several years by a very ill-defined policy in relation with the importation of foreign textiles on the domestic market.
On several occasions, over the years, I had the privilege of meeting the textile workers and each time, they told me about the enormous difficulties they have in this industry, and they have always tried to make us aware of the problems they face, not only myself but all those who have a responsibility to act at any level, whether at the public level, at the level of civil servants or at the level of legislators.
The excellent paper recently prepared by the CSD on the difficulties in the Canadian textile industry, in which they make a final attempt, was brought to the attention of legislators and the general public. A large effort was made, Mr. Speaker, to make the government concerned about the real causes of the difficulties and problems facing the textile industry in Quebec, mostly in the Eastern Townships.
The government would do better considering in a positive way the findings of the paper made public a few weeks ago already by the Centrale des syndicats demo-cratiques which deals rather thoroughly with all aspects of the problem we are faced with in this extremely important domestic industry. Several short term solutions are proposed in this paper, but long term alternatives are also taken into consideration. It is interesting to note that the suggestions made last year in the House reappear in one form or another in the recommendations which followed certain studies made across the country, especially in Quebec, on the way to improve the conditions of workers in the Canadian textile industry.
Obviously we must find a long term global strategy for this industry, I mean a development strategy which would enable the Canadian textile industry to become really competition-oriented. This industry has never been given the opportunity to become competitive and stand up to foreign goods.
As I have said previously, the Eastern Townships are dominated by the textile industry. In fact over 20 per cent of all industrial jobs in Quebec depend directly or indirectly upon it. In the Eastern Townships, this ratio is even higher in some cases and reach over 50 per cent. We should be concerned about the future of these areas where this sector employs such a large proportion of workers if we consider that the textile industry in general has not during the last few years grown according to the expectations of the early 70's.
One must add, in the same breath, that in 1970 the textile industry was given a certain direction which was a few years later sort of put aside by an importation policy obviously contrary to the bills passed by Parliament. Some time ago, we tried to change the textile industry into a consistent and dynamic industry so that it could eventually compete, but when one realizes the present conditions of this industry, and the lack of encouragement from government policies, one feels that it would be catastrophic at this time to allow exchange liberalization in this industry.
If we do not protect the textile industry against foreign competition, we might well find, within a few years, an industry almost dead or so weak that it would not be able to outlive any effect of competition. For now, we must absolutely forget about exchange liberalization because this industry itself has no defence. On equal terms, it would be fair if the textile industry could compete on the international level, but as it is in an unfavourable position to begin with, it is cruel and unfair not to give the appropriate tools to an industry which we want prosperous and dynamic.
Some officials are reported to have been entrusted a few months ago by a cabinet committee with a complete review of the Canadian textile policy. Over a month ago, a Senate committee was conducting a study on the textile situation in Canada. More recently, about a month ago, a committee was set up to look into the whole Canadian textile industry and to report before June 30. The terms of reference of the special advisory committee appointed by the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, whose report is to be submitted by June 30, was instructed to look into the present conditions, the outlook and the trade position of the textile and clothing industry, to review the policy with regard to competitive imports, and also to consider the opportunity, under the present legislation and instruments, of implementing a policy with regards to paragraphs 3 and 4 of the 19th GATT agreement, and to report its conclusions and recommendations to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce by June 30, 1976.
I hope, Mr. Speaker, that all the reports of those committees, commissions and task forces which will be submitted very shortly, will not remain a dead letter. We should not once again give glimmers of hope to textile workers and union members. People do not always live on glimmers of hope, and for so many years, that is what has been happening in this area. It is also time that someone answered some stupid comments made recently by two Canadian high officials who admitted in rather clear terms that the textile industry should eventually disappear or be considerably reduced in Canada.
Mr. Raynauld, president of the Economic Council of Canada and Mr. Joe Morris, president of the largest labour congress in Canada made those comments without really knowing the problem. The day when we no longer have a textile industry in this country, we will no longer have a viable industry in Canada. We will then have to pay a lot more for our clothing than we do at present.
The Canadian textile industry has a tremendous potential if it is allowed to develop as it can. Salaries have increased and even though they do not compare with those paid in other sectors, they are nevertheless interesting. There is also another matter I would like to raise briefly, and it has to do with the labelling and the enormous frauds that the Department of Trade, Industry and Commerce apparently fails to see. In certain cases, it was pointed out that "Made in Taiwan" labels and "Made in Korea" labels were exhanged and simply replaced with "Made in Canada" labels: Goods not made in this country were labelled as such and displayed in Canadian stores; that is what is known as outright fraud.
The department of Manpower is involved in the textile industry and so is the Department of National Revenue,

June 3, 1976

through customs and excise, the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, the Department of Labour and many others. But when you get down to the bottom of it, you really wonder whether one of those departments can, through its own policy, allow the textile industry to make progress. As has been pointed out in last year's intervention, the problem may be easier than it is believed. What the textile industry and the workers in that sector are asking for is the assurance of an increasing part of the market to eventually reach 75 or 80 per cent of the Canadian market.
Now, Canadian manufacturers have 46 per cent of our market. The government, through the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, indicates that close to 75 per cent of the market is controlled by Canadian manufacturers. Which of the two are we to believe? We do not even know, statistically speaking, whether those 46 per cent of the Canadian market the textile workers say they hold or the 75 per cent the government says belongs to the Canadian manufacturers are true figures. It is startling to note a difference of 30 per cent between the figures quoted by one and those quoted by the other.
We must therefore after all be happy that a detailed study is now being conducted on the future prospects of the textile industry and that if it truly has a future, the government will review its business policy and its global policy in this area, provided of course it really wants this sector, which is so important for Quebec and all of Canada, to survive. It is essential that the government stop allowing the countries who are much better placed to do so to compete against domestic industries.
A little over a year ago, the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Chretien) told textile union members who had come to Ottawa that the government had no intention of letting the textile industry die out. However, when we see that imports have increased, that the Canadian share of the market is not even 50 per cent, if we believe this figure, we must ask ourselves if all the necessary action is being taken to allow this industry to live or to survive.
In the textile area, there has been a higher productivity rate than in any other industrial sector since 1953. And in 20 years, this sector has had lower prices than any other sector. In my humble opinion, there are certainly solutions to the problems that I have just described. There are answers to all the complaints that have been made these last few years, but to this day, the answers have not been satisfying for the simple reason that the government does not follow up on what it says.
A great part of our imports now come from the United States. Yet we are well aware that the Americans can compete very strongly on the Canadian market. We must give our manufacturers the means to defend themselves. If we want true competition, let us give Canadian producers a useful instrument to allow them to compete efficiently and equally, and I am convinced that the Canadian producers will fare well.
At the present time, one of the great problems of the textile industry is the lack of information and discussion among the various levels. We are told that the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce has some 25 employees dealing day after day with the textile industry. Those 25 employees must make sure that the 200,000 workers in that
The Budget-Mr. Dick
sector earn a decent living. I sincerely believe that if those 25 individuals really want to look conscientiously and dynamically after that sector, they will have done much for the textile industry.
From now on, we will have to check whether the persons dealing with the textile industry, at any level whatever, especially at the federal level, make the necessary suggestions to the pertinent department for the development of that sector. On several occasions in recent years the government has indicated its intention of helping Canadian industry. Is it necessary to point out that the textile industry is 90 per cent Canadian. The fine intentions and kind words stated during those last years must now be translated into action.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) stated that one of the best ways to increase industrial productivity is to encourage the development of high technology and innovative new processes. He then went on to say that this is a high risk business and a difficult one into which to attract venture capital. However, the result of this statement by the minister was only a promise to have his officials study this matter on a priority basis, whatever and whenever that might be.
In comparison to this lukewarm decision to make a study into something which he says is important, may I read into the record the official position of the Progressive Conservative party:
The Progressive Conservative Party believes expenditures on research and development are capital expenditures-investments in the future. We believe that, like all investments, if wisely made they will yield tremendous dividends. Our party has faith in Canada and the skills of Canadians and would make large-scale productive investments in science and technology.
We have a commitment and a belief. Let us compare it to the statement in a press release from the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce on May 10, 1976, to the effect that after providing more than $220 million in research and development funds to do something for Canadian companies during the last nine years, the Industrial Research and Development Incentives Act will end this year.
The budget also referred to some deductions for small business. The minister indicated that these measures would significantly benefit all small- and medium-sized corporations. I should like to suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, and to members of this House that these promises of measures which will be of some small assistance to small business do not go to the core of the problem and of course will do nothing to help research and development which is so desperately needed if we are to expand the industrial base in this country. Canada needs a good research and development policy. Canada needs an industrial strategy unless we are to settle for a role as a second or third class industrial and scientific community.
On June 9, 1975, a member on the government side, the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Philbrook), stated that a national science policy for Canada of grand design has been seriously considered for many years by all interested

June 3, 1976
The Budget-Mr. Dick
parties, especially since science and technology began to dominate our lives after World War II as the spearhead for all society and our whole way of life. He said there has also been criticism in Canada of such a policy, mainly in that we have not been able to formulate one and therefore we have tended to fall behind other nations in scientific, political economic clout.
In September of 1975 the part-time minister, or as was explained earlier this session in a debate on science, the minister who spends four hours per week on science and technology, announced the publication of a report entitled "The Availability of Risk Capital for Technological Innovation and Invention in Canada". This report indicated what he says is a severe shortage in Canada of high risk investment which should be available to support technological ventures because we do not have the incentives for people to invest in high risk investments.
What do we have? We have some foreign controlled groups, mostly American, coming in and buying out our technology and our companies. There are not the incentives for Canadians to do this. A few years ago the government indicated that it would slow down the process, and of course it introduced FIRA. What has happened is that under the Foreign Investment Review Act about 85 per cent of all applications by foreign-controlled consortiums to buy Canadian companies have been approved by the government. So really the government has not done very much. There has been a lot of talk and much hot air but not much of substance has been provided. In the area in which it has proudly proclaimed it spent $220 million in research and development funds since 1967 to some 3,000 Canadian companies, it has now decided to wipe that out.
The Industrial Research and Development Incentives Act made its debut in 1967 to provide for the payment of outright cash grants, based on expenditures in Canada for scientific research and development by a taxable corporation in its fiscal year. The Industrial Research and Development Incentives Act also provided grants to universities, colleges, research institutions, and non-profit Canadian corporations. Those grants were exempt from income tax in order to emphasize that they were an additional incentive offered to Canadian industry and were designed to supplement the normal deductions of all research and development expenditures allowed under the Income Tax Act. Now, as part of these draconian cuts in government spending that we have heard so much about, IRDIA has been dropped. In order to try to gain some measure of restraint today, the government has cut out possible growth in the future arising from a scientific and technologically superior industrial base.
The IRDIA program was the only government assistance program that I am aware of that gave support to new business, except perhaps in the special DREE areas, and it is one of the very few programs that gave capital equipment assistance at any time. This was particularly helpful to small businesses as a new venture incentive where capital was necessary because of the technology involved.
The response to the program over the years has been warm. Many Canadian companies have applied for grants. The response to the repeal of this act was overwhelming.
[Mr. Dick.)
The Chairman of the Science Council of Canada has countered that technology based industries in Canada must be accorded a National priority. The Chairman of the Department of Geology at the University of Toronto has stated that, just as earth sciences became most exciting, funds for Canadian research were cut. The Chairman of the Science Policy Committee of the Canadian Association of Physicists has stated that Canadian physics is in a depression. The Chairman of the Department of Medical Genetics at the University of Toronto has said:
The government's policy in this respect could produce serious repercussions by undermining the quality of the universities, restricting opportunities for young people and limiting our ability to meet the challenges of our technological society and that Canada is indeed on the way to becoming a second or even a third-rate scientific community.
The Chairman of the Department of Medical Genetics at the University of Toronto was perhaps speaking in the area in which he has most knowledge, but he stated something that applied to all young people in Canada when he said that this action of the government will have "serious repercussions by undermining the quality of universities". But most important, Mr. Speaker, is the following phrase, "restricting opportunities for young people". We cannot employ the young people in our country today. There are people with Ph.Ds who cannot get jobs; there are engineers who cannot find employment; there are people with B.As who cannot work in any of fields for which they have been trained, and this is because we are expanding our industrial base rather than our scientific and research base.
Not so very long ago the Senate Special Committee on Science Policy under the chairmanship of Senator Maurice Lamontagne made an exhaustive study of Canada's research and development efforts with respect to this country's economic needs, and issued a three volume report entitled "A Science Policy for Canada". The third volume recommended that Canada should steadily increase its support of research and development and achieve by 1980 a figure of 2.5 per cent of our gross national product. A corresponding increase should have been made for support of basic research.
A recent Statistics Canada survey of "leading performers" showed that the in-house research and development expenditures as a percentage of the gross national product have declined in terms of current dollars to about .37 per cent in 1973 from .44 per cent in 1967. Mr. Speaker, .37 per cent is a long way from the 2.5 per cent which was predicted as needed if we were going to be a first class technology based industrial nation.
For some reason we have not been able to formulate a national science policy. The government has not put forth a science policy, and we have tended to fall behind all other nations in scientific-political-economic clout. We live in a more and more technical society and must make judgments on areas such as food supply, pollution, population control, energy resources, and nuclear disarmament. The decisions made by Canada are limited by our appreciation of what science can and cannot achieve.
With regard to industrial technology we have a minister who is urging Canadian businessmen to go outside Canada to form joint ventures with the Third World and export back to Canada something which is just taking jobs away from Canadians, as has happened under Bill C-179 in the twenty-ninth parliament. I know of a certain factory in my
June 3, 1976

constituency of Lanark-Renfrew-Carleton which went out of business because of it. Some 400 people were formerly employed there.
What we should be doing is staying in our own country, developing what we have. We are not doing much to encourage development of manufactured products in this country. If we are to maintain a strong industrial base then we can assist others, but if we weaken our home base surely we are going to be in grave danger.
The OECD has indicated that of the 12 countries spending various percentages of their Gross National Product on research and development, Canada stands tenth, behind the United States, France, United Kingdom, Sweden, Germany, The Netherlands, Belgium, Japan, and Norway. Mr. Speaker, perhaps I may call it ten o'clock and continue at the next calling of this debate.
A motion to adjourn the House under Standing Order 40 deemed to have been moved.

subtopic: AGRICULTURE-REQUEST FOR REPORT ON STUDY OF EFFECT OF REMOVAL OF FREIGHT SUBSIDY ON WHEAT AND FLOUR FOR EXPORT
AGRICULTURE-REQUEST FOR REPORT ON STUDY OF EFFECT OF REMOVAL OF FREIGHT SUBSIDY ON WHEAT AND FLOUR FOR EXPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think this is the fifth, sixth, or perhaps even the seventh time that on the late show of this parliament I have raised the question of the proposal under Bill C-87 to do away with the subsidies on the transportation of flour and ground cereals through Atlantic and eastern Canadian ports under the Railway Act.
One of the advantages of being so persistent-along with other members who have done the same thing-is that it seems on the late show we have tended to find out where the issues really are. After talking and arguing with the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang), the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Chretien), the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan), the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Jamieson), and all of the hon. gentlemen I brought into the picture on the late show, I gather it really boils down to the fact that the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce are very much in my corner, and the President of the Treasury Board is willing to pat me on the head and say he is in my corner because it is a substantial issue, but he knows that he has to carry out the financial mandate of the government. The Minister of Transport is squarely against me.
On the other hand the Minister of Transport has made this much of a concession, that since the debate started- not before the debate started-we have had smuggled into this issue the question of the unit train concept, that is, that there would be a train which would leave some Sas-
Adjournment Debate
katchewan or Manitoba grain point every so often and make its way to Halifax, or to Saint John, for that matter, and there unload its cargo for delivery overseas. So this much at least we have got of the Minister of Transport.
Now, mind you, we have no guarantee that this is going to happen, and it is because we have no guarantee that I continue to put my skeptical six foot four inch self up in the House of Commons from time to time to try to argue this issue. I think it is important to the port of Halifax, but also the port of Saint John, to the port of Montreal, to any number of communities in Ontario where there are flour mills, and to the wheat producers of western Canada.
Lest somebody should ever dare to tell me that I am arguing a very special interest to the port of Halifax, this has been discussed in an article which is part of a series of articles written by Ian Thompson, who is the transportation reporter for the Halifax Chronicle-Herald and for the Mail-Star, and who I think has done a pretty fair job of trying to analyse the situation. These articles can be found in those two newspapers for the week of approximately May 20 to May 26. In any event, quoting from the last part:
In 1975 the St. Lawrence Seaway handled about 450 million bushels of wheat from Canadian and American fields, more than 20 times that which went through the Port of Halifax.
Even if Halifax were operated to capacity and the additional business was taken from the Seaway, river ports would still be left with over 400 million bushels, more than six times that of a busy Halifax.
So I hope by putting that fact as succinctly as I could on record it is evident that I am not trying to argue that Halifax should have any enormous advantage over Montreal or any other place like that. I am not, but I am arguing, I will continue to argue, and perhaps I will be arguing into August because that is how strongly I feel about clause 15 of Bill C-87. Halifax at least should be permitted its legal place in the Canadian sun. It need not be permitted a great, great place, but at least nothing which is less than other places enjoy.
I asked the Minister of Agriculture my question the other day, and it is his minion who will be replying tonight. The question I asked was: what about the studies which are being carried out in the Department of Agriculture? Obviously the Minister of Agriculture looked at me with a friendly eye. As a matter of fact, both of them were friendly the other day when he answered my question. I do not know what kind of response I will receive tonight from the person who reports for him, but the fact is that there have been studies carried out there, and very properly.
There should have been studies carried out within the Department of Agriculture on the effect of the proposed cutting out of that particular subsidy under section 272 of the Railway Act. The minister is obviously in my corner, but he also obviously is not here tonight. However, I am just hoping that he and the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce will start to exert a greater amount of influence within the cabinet on this matter. We face Bill C-87. I put it this way-I do not mind at all having unit trains to Halifax. I can understand that; it will be a noble experiment. But let the train be in situ, as it were, in operation, before something which means so much to the waterfront of a great Canadian port is cut out.
14148

June 3, 1976
Adjournment Debate

speakeroldname: Mr. Irenee Pelletier (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: AGRICULTURE-REQUEST FOR REPORT ON STUDY OF EFFECT OF REMOVAL OF FREIGHT SUBSIDY ON WHEAT AND FLOUR FOR EXPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on looking over the official report. I found that this matter has been discussed at least six times during the adjournment debate since April. Answers to this question have been given by the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare on March 22, 1976, by the Minister of Transport himself on April 5, 1976, by the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce on April 13, by the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board on April 29, 1976 and by myself on March 29 and 30. Therefore, there are very few new developments of which I can inform the House at this stage.
As regards the question that the hon. member put to the Minister of Agriculture on May 27, I can inform the House that studies are presently being carried out within the department. These studies are pursued in co-operation with the Canadian Grains Commission, the Canadian Wheat Board and other federal departments.
The Canadian Grains Commission has assured the minister on several occasions that the storage requirements in Atlantic ports will be fully safeguarded. The Canadian Wheat Board believes that Canadian grain exports will not be affected by the removal of this subsidy. Discussions have also taken place in the House about the use of unit trains for the movement of grain from the Prairies to the Atlantic ports.
Nevertheless, Mr. Speaker, I wish to inform the House that this matter is still under review and that our department, the Department of Agriculture, is giving it close attention, and that discussions are under way in order to ensure that such action will have no adverse effect. The minister has already made these undertakings to the Canadian National Millers' Association.

subtopic: THE QUEEN-DATE OF STATEMENT ON PLANS TO CELEBRATE HER MAJESTY'S SILVER JUBILEE
THE QUEEN-DATE OF STATEMENT ON PLANS TO CELEBRATE HER MAJESTY'S SILVER JUBILEE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise this evening to draw the attention of the House to the fact that 1977 will mark the Silver Jubilee of our Queen's reign.

subtopic: THE QUEEN-DATE OF STATEMENT ON PLANS TO CELEBRATE HER MAJESTY'S SILVER JUBILEE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: THE QUEEN-DATE OF STATEMENT ON PLANS TO CELEBRATE HER MAJESTY'S SILVER JUBILEE
speechtext:
What an occasion for celebration, the celebration of Thanksgiving for the 25 years of Her Majesty's service and dedication to her peoples, service given in love, without any reward save that of knowing that she has accomplished thoroughly and well that which, as the young princess, she promised to do on her twenty-first birthday: that all her life, long or short, would be dedicated to our service. Has ever a vow been more conscientiously or faithfully maintained?
The Secretary of State (Mr. Faulkner) told the House that a committee is working on plans to celebrate this event in Canada and that he may be in a position to make a statement to the House some time this month as to plans for celebrating this great event. Seeing that the plans for the celebrations in the United Kingdom were announced

last December, it is evident that Her Majesty's Canadian ministers are already well behind the times.
I venture to make some suggestions to the committee on behalf of the average Canadian who loves his sovereign lady and who, perhaps more important, has a profound respect for the role played by the institution of the Crown-

subtopic: THE QUEEN-DATE OF STATEMENT ON PLANS TO CELEBRATE HER MAJESTY'S SILVER JUBILEE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: THE QUEEN-DATE OF STATEMENT ON PLANS TO CELEBRATE HER MAJESTY'S SILVER JUBILEE
speechtext:
-that democratic system we cherish, embodied in the constitutional monarchy. That average Canadian, Mr. Speaker, would like to see celebrations both of substantial importance and of symbolic significance.
To deal with the first, I suggest that the government take upon itself, maybe with the helpful advice of loyal societies such as the IODE, the Monarchist League, the United Empire Loyalist Association, and the Royal Canadian Legion, the task of disseminating widely across Canada information about the role played by the Crown in our lives. By the end of 1977 every child should have gained a new perspective on our system of government, and doubtless many of their elders will have learned a few things too.
This widespread distribution of information should naturally be complimented by a host of symbolic events up and down the breadth of this dominion-national services of Thanksgiving in churches and synagogues across the country; a national bonfire coast to coast on the evening of the accession; fireworks displays on Victoria Day; dedication or re-dedication of federal parks, buildings and other sites in honour of our Queen; the enshrining by statute of "God Save the Queen" as the Royal Anthem and "O Canada" as the National Anthem; the issuance of a special stamp and coin series and the appropriate replacement of the present abstract design which appears in lieu of Her Majesty's portrait on pre-stamped envelopes; a symbolic meeting of the Queen's Privy Council for Canada after all, we are the only commonwealth country to have its own privy council-and, finally, a full royal tour. Let us not confine our Queen to Ottawa, but remember that as Queen of all Canada she should be allowed to visit, however briefly, all parts of her realm, for it is all sections of this dominion which desire to do her homage.
When Her Majesty comes to Ottawa, I trust that her government will see to it that an opportunity is given for the Queen of Canada to perform in public the important constitutional duties of our sovereign; to open or to prorogue a parliament, and to give Royal Assent to bills. In this way our constitutional abstraction is made a living reality.
