subtopic: ENERGY-DISPUTE BETWEEN NEWFOUNDLAND AND QUEBEC OVER CHURCHILL FALLS POWER-ACTION OF MINISTER
ENERGY-DISPUTE BETWEEN NEWFOUNDLAND AND QUEBEC OVER CHURCHILL FALLS POWER-ACTION OF MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on March 31 I questioned the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie) about the dispute between the provinces of Newfoundland and Quebec with regard to the request by Newfoundland to recall some 800 megawatts of electric power from the Churchill Falls power station, a portion of the 5,225 total production which was negotiated for sale to Quebec by the previous government of Newfoundland.
The power is urgently required to develop the Lower Churchill-Gull Island site, particularly for the construction of transmission lines in the tunnel, in order to transmit same for the needs of the province in its future development, the creation of jobs and, indeed, to help Canada in its vital energy requirements.
Under a 65 year contract signed with Hydro Quebec in 1969, Newfoundland is entitled to recall 300 megawatts, but the province needs 800 megawatts. It is obvious that the federal government recognizes the justification of the lower Churchill development as it offered to provide some $343 million, out of a total $1 billion, in loans to the province.
I feel that in the interest of Canada, in the words of the premier of Newfoundland, it is particularly galling that Quebec is making enormous profits from the power sold to them at a ridiculous cost. More galling to me is their refusal to act as good partners in Confederation or to contribute toward solving the national problem, particularly when this could be done without hardship to the Quebec economy. It is total blackmail when the responsible Quebec minister states that a condition for acceding to Newfoundland's request would be the sale to Quebec of land comprising the watersheds of the five rivers which rise in Labrador and which flow through Quebec into the Gulf of St. Lawrence.
Under the agreement of 1969 the province of Quebec pays 3.5 mills per kilowatt hour and sell it for prices which range from 24 mills to 42 mills. While I realize that from an
Adjournment Debate
economic point of view Quebec cannot be blamed for taking advantage of a good thing, and that one cannot blame the previous administration in Newfoundland which might be criticized for entering into a bad deal, particularly when we recall that in 1969 predictions made by experts indicated that Canada had an abundance of energy available for use into the distant future, what I am concerned about, Mr. Speaker, is that the minister seemed to be reluctant to enter into these negotiations or to make any effort to impress on the Quebec government the need for a change in its attitude toward Premier Moore's request made in the national interest.
I emphasize that the premier has been more than cooperative. In the message he sent to the premier of Quebec he said, first, that he hoped an equitable and amicable arrangement could be concluded and that he was ready to undertake negotiations with respect to right of access to Churchill Falls power with a fairer apportionment of the benefits to both provinces. In the second place, he expressed willingness to agree to the joint development of the rivers which are common to Newfoundland and Quebec as part of the fuller use of Labrador hydro resources.
Needless to say, while the government of Newfoundland has expressed every willingness to co-operate, it is adamant in taking the position that, if the dog in the manger attitude of the Quebec government persists, there are other courses of action which can be taken. Under clause 2 (E) of the agreement giving the lessee the right to transmit throughout the province and to export such power, there is a provision that, upon the request of the Newfoundland government, its consumers of electricity shall be given priority where it is feasible and economic to do so. Unless agreement is reached the government of Newfoundland has no alternative but to institute steps to seek clarification of its legal rights, and once right of access is established the province could conceivably take the entire output of Churchill Falls.
My purpose in speaking tonight is to impress on the minister and upon the government that they should address themselves to this issue immediately rather than continue the passive interest which they have shown up to now. I say this Because of the need, as a priority, to develop alternative sourcek of power which are available through the Lower Churchill Gull Island project so as to relieve the pressures of the energy shortage for the benefit of our nation. I ask the minister to recognize the contribution which Newfoundland could make to this end, a contribution which is being hindered by one of the Canadian partners in Confederation.
I can only hope the minister or the parliamentary secretary will express, on behalf of the government, a willingness to direct meaningful attention to this problem in the interest of Canada and of national unity.
